releases.headline: A self-hosted mail server that runs as one container
releases.summary: blamepost serves SMTP, IMAP, JMAP, POP3, ManageSieve and a browser interface from a single process against a single data volume. Mail arrives over SMTP, is authenticated at DATA, filtered by the recipient's Sieve script, and is readable over IMAP, JMAP and POP3 or in the browser. Mail leaves over one policy chain that resolves the receiver, enforces MTA-STS, classifies what the far side said, retries on its own schedule and reports a permanent failure back to the account that sent it. There are no npm runtime dependencies: the framework it composes is vendored in the tarball you install. Read ROADMAP.md before deploying: it marks every capability shipped, targeted, planned or under design, and it ships in that tarball beside the README.

items.title: One process, every protocol an operator's clients speak
items.body: Port 25 accepts inbound mail, 587 and 465 accept authenticated submission over STARTTLS and implicit TLS, 143 serves IMAP4rev2, 4190 serves ManageSieve, and 8080 and 8443 serve the browser interface, the administration surface and JMAP. POP3 on 110 is off unless you turn it on. Every mail listener requires TLS and none has a plaintext mode, so the server refuses to start without a certificate and key. The browser port on 8080 is the one that stays cleartext, because it is what a container health check and a proxy in front poll, and a session is not reachable over it: the session cookie is only ever sent back over TLS. Nothing binds 993 or 995: IMAP and POP3 negotiate TLS in band here, and a terminator in front of 143 or 110 does not stand in for that, because the listener is handed an unencrypted connection and refuses every credential offered over it. Port 25 does not bind while no domain is hosted, so a server that is running but not yet configured does not answer for recipients it knows nothing about, and the reason it declined is in the log and in the audit trail; the mailbox listeners and the browser interface come up regardless, which is how you finish the setup. An unacknowledged DNS posture is the stronger refusal and stops the whole boot rather than one listener, so BLAMEPOST_DNS_ACKNOWLEDGED and each hosted domain's own acknowledgment come before anything serves at all. Turning the MX listener off is the one setting that skips that question, because then nothing is accepting mail for the records to answer for. Each listener's port is individually overridable, which is how you run it behind standard host ports without giving the process any Linux capability. So are the ceilings every listener holds against one source address: how many connections that address may hold at once, and the connection, authentication-failure and refused-recipient rates. The largest message accepted is settable beside them and bounds one message rather than one address, on ports 25, 465 and 587 alone. The defaults suit a peer delivering mail rather than a mailbox client, and the operator guide explains which one to raise when your users sit behind a single address.

items.title: Inbound mail is authenticated before it is accepted
items.body: SPF, DKIM verification, DMARC and the ARC chain all run at DATA, and the verdict is written into the Authentication-Results header your clients and filters read. HELO discipline and forward-confirmed reverse DNS run at the connection. Every one of those lookups goes through the one resolver this server holds rather than each gate building its own, so the connection checks and the message checks read a single view of the zone instead of two that can disagree. That resolver is built with the strict profile, which decides how an answer is parsed and bounded rather than where the question goes. Where it goes is the vendored framework's default, a public DNS-over-HTTPS endpoint. No setting here names a different one: neither the configuration file nor any BLAMEPOST_ variable reaches it, and the only substitution available is passing `blamepost.create` a resolver of your own, which means embedding this server rather than running the image. So every SPF, DKIM, DMARC and HELO lookup this server makes leaves the machine to that endpoint, and that endpoint sees every name a peer causes this server to ask about. It is the same resolver you are vouching for when you set `outboundPolicy.dnssecValidated: true` so `dane: "enforce"` will run. A domain that publishes no policy is scored as having no policy, not as a temporary DNS failure, so mail from it is not deferred at the wire.

items.title: Submission is bound to the authenticated identity
items.body:
An account may only send as an address it owns. A MAIL FROM for anything else is refused with 553 5.7.1 before a single recipient is accepted, and the session survives the refusal so a client that guesses wrong once can correct itself. This is not a policy option. An authenticated account that could send as any address is an open relay with extra steps.

The address a person actually reads is bound as well. Every address this server hosts, whether it is named in the From header or in a Sender header, has to be one the account may write: its own address, or an alias that points at it, with a subaddress tag folding to the address it extends. Where a message names several authors, every one of them at a domain this server hosts has to qualify, since a list mixing your address with a colleague's is the forgery rather than an exception to it, and at least one of the addresses named has to be yours. An author at a domain hosted elsewhere is left alone, so writing on behalf of an outside correspondent still works: this server's key creates no alignment for a domain it does not host, and that domain's own policy answers for it. A message carrying no From header, or a second From or Sender header, is refused whatever it names. Refusals happen before the message is signed, and the audit trail carries the identity that was rejected alongside the ones that would have been accepted. The client is answered 451 4.3.0, which is the only reply a refused handoff can produce, so the reason it cannot carry is in the log and in that row rather than on the wire.

items.title: Sieve runs at delivery, and scripts are managed over ManageSieve
items.body: The recipient's active script runs against every message that arrives for them, from a peer and from a local sender alike, under a gas budget so a pathological script cannot burn delivery-path processor time without bound. A script is validated before it is stored. Actions that would put a message on the wire keep the message and record the refusal instead of dropping it, so the account holder still gets their mail and you can see what was asked for and not done. Scripts are uploaded, listed, fetched, renamed, activated and deleted over ManageSieve on 4190. `blamepost account sieve` reads what an account holds; it takes a reason and records that an administrator opened somebody's filter, so it is one of the verbs that needs the server stopped. The browser interface does not edit them, so an account holder who wants filtering needs a ManageSieve client.

items.title: One deletion path, with a retention floor and legal hold in front of it
items.body: IMAP EXPUNGE, the POP3 QUIT that applies a session's DELEs, JMAP Email/set destroyed and the browser interface's own purge all route through the same gate, so a message refused on one surface is refused on all of them, an account erasure included. Set BLAMEPOST_COMPLIANCE_POSTURE to soc2 for a one year floor below which a hard delete is refused, for the account owner as much as for an administrator, measured from the moment this server filed the message rather than from any date a client supplied with it. A message under legal hold survives regardless: the client is not told it went, a later session still finds it, and the body is still readable. With no posture set the floor is zero and legal hold is the only thing that keeps a message, which is what most operators want.

items.title: IMAP search answers or refuses, and never returns an empty set it cannot stand behind
items.body: A client searching a mailbox gets a real answer for the keys this server can evaluate: flags and keywords, arrival dates, sizes, sequence and identifier sets, subject, sender, the To addresses, the header fields it stores, and any boolean combination of those, matching on substrings as the specification requires rather than on whole words. For a key it cannot evaluate it refuses and names the key: the Cc and Bcc addresses, the body and whole-message keys, and the dates a message says it was sent on, as against the dates it arrived on. That property matters more than the list does. A search that quietly returns nothing tells the account holder their mailbox has no matches, and leaves them no way to discover the question was never asked. Most of the keys that refuse are the ones whose data this server does not keep, and every refusal names the key and says why. A HEADER key naming a field the store does not keep refuses the same way the named keys do, and so does a charset this server cannot read a term in. One limit is not about stored data at all: the extended result form RETURN asks for is not served, on either spelling of the command. A second one is about how a term arrives rather than what it asks. A term carried as a literal reaches the search on SEARCH and is dropped on UID SEARCH, so the UID form answers BAD because the key it was written for has nothing after it. A client sending a non-ASCII term usually sends it as a literal and usually asks for the UID form, so the two meet: write such a term inline until the framework's UID dispatch carries a literal through to the handler.

items.title: POP3 gives the maildrop to one session at a time and releases it on idleness
items.body: RFC 1939 allows one session per maildrop, so this server hands it to whoever opens it first and refuses everybody else until that session is finished. A session finishes cleanly by sending QUIT. One that loses its connection instead is released after thirty minutes with nothing happening on it, measured from the last command rather than from when the session started, so a long download is never taken away from the client still running it. Deletions apply only at QUIT, which means an interrupted session deletes nothing and offers the same mail again on the next collection. Holds live in memory and write nothing to the data volume, so a restart releases every one of them and there is no lock file to clear by hand. The operator guide covers what to tell an account holder whose client reports the mailbox in use.

items.title: An account can write as an address it holds, in the browser and over JMAP
items.body: A shared departmental address pointed at somebody's mailbox is an address they can send as, not only one they receive at. The compose form offers the choice only where there is one, so a mailbox owner with a single address sees the form they always saw, and JMAP returns one sending identity per permitted address so a client can present the same choice. The set is the account's own address plus every active alias pointed straight at it, with a subaddress folding to the address it extends and a catch-all never counting, since a catch-all claims every name in the domain. It follows one alias row rather than a chain, so an address that reaches the mailbox by way of a second alias is delivered there and is still not one the account may write. The picker is presentation only: the server recomputes the set on every send and writes the address from that set rather than the one the request carried, so nothing a form submitted reaches the header. The return path stays the account's own address, which is what lets this work at all; a desktop client on the submission port derives the envelope from its configured identity and puts the alias in both places, and the envelope binding refuses that.

items.title: A browser interface for mailbox owners and for you
items.body:
Read, search, compose, reply, reply to all, forward, move, flag, mark read, trash and purge, rendered on the server with client JavaScript as opt-in islands rather than a required runtime. Creating, renaming and deleting a folder is not offered, on any protocol. Remote and active content in a message is treated as hostile: images are held back until the reader asks for them, and asking reveals them for that message alone. The sign-in form takes fifty posts from one source address in five minutes and refuses that address for the rest of the window.

The administration surface covers domains, accounts, aliases, DKIM selectors, sign-in lockouts, the outbound queue and the audit log. It is held to the machine and browser the session was opened on: a request whose client address, browser or accepted language does not match the session is asked for the password again. The session row is kept, so the account carries on reading its mail and a failed attempt does not end the session. A mailbox session is not held that way: a phone moving between wifi and a cell network changes address, and mail stays open across the change.

items.title: The operator role is given to an existing account and taken back, from the console
items.body:
`blamepost init` creates an account carrying the operator role, and the account page in the administration interface is where an account that already exists is given it and where it is taken away again. Both of those controls ask for a reason before anything changes and both write a row: `blamepost audit read --action account.role_granted` and `--action account.role_revoked`. The create form on the same page carries a checkbox that gives a new account the role as it is made. That one asks for no reason and writes no grant row, so it reaches the trail as `account.created` with the role recorded on it, and an operator asking who was ever handed the console reads that action alongside the other two. The two row controls are not mirror images. A grant is offered and accepted only on an account that is in service, while the control that takes the role back sits on any row holding it whatever that row's status says, which the entry on granting the role sets out along with why.

Taking the role back is the narrow answer to an administrator whose credential has been taken, and to one who has moved on. It reaches a session that account already has open rather than waiting for the session to expire, because every request reads the role off the account row rather than off the session record. It leaves the mailbox signing in, sending and receiving, so answering a stolen password does not stop mail for a person whose mailbox was not the problem. The console will not let the last one go: taking the role from an account, suspending it, archiving it and disabling the domain its address belongs to are each measured against who would still be able to sign in afterwards, and each is refused when the answer is nobody. The refusal is recorded, at `blamepost audit read --action blamepost.web.last_administrator_removal_not_permitted`, and the way past it is to give the role to somebody else first.

A grant is the widest thing this server hands out, so the page says what it hands over: every mailbox owner's address, every hosted domain, the outbound spool, the signing keys and this audit trail, along with archiving an account and stopping a domain taking mail. It hands over nobody's messages. There is no command line verb for either direction; `init` grants the role while creating an account rather than on one that already exists, and the operator guide says so where it says how to recover a console nobody can sign in to.

items.title: An operator command line that answers questions
items.body: serve, init, account, domain, dkim, queue, doctor, audit, backup, restore and blobs. There is no alias verb among them: an address that forwards into a mailbox is added and withdrawn on the administration interface's aliases page. `account list` answers with the mailboxes that are still in the picture, which is the active ones, the suspended ones and any part way through an erasure, because the question an operator usually has is which mailboxes are live; `--include-archived` adds the archived rows, and that is where the address `account resume` takes back is found. doctor resolves your live DNS posture and names precisely which record is wrong rather than reporting a general failure. queue shows what is waiting, why, and what the far side actually said; `queue show <id>` narrows that to one message, every attempt made on it and how it ends if nothing changes. audit verifies the audit chain has not been truncated or rolled back and exports a range for an auditor. backup takes a verified encrypted backup and restore puts one back, with a rollback path if the restore itself fails. blobs compares the stored message bodies against the rows that reference them, and with verification turned on it unseals and re-hashes every one, so a body altered or truncated under a file nobody rewrites is found by you rather than by the account holder who opens the message. Almost every verb that destroys takes a recorded reason, and the ones that destroy in bulk take `--confirm` on top of it: reclaiming the bodies nothing references, purging the audit trail or a backup set, releasing a preservation order, and putting a restore or a rollback in place. Erasing an account and removing a domain name the destruction instead, with `--destroy` beside the reason: `account remove` without it archives the mailbox and keeps its mail, and `domain disable` is what stops mail for a domain without losing anything. Two verbs take no reason at all, and both destroy sealed signing keys: `blamepost dkim retire` and `blamepost dkim sweep`, because the row each writes carries what the signer said about the run rather than a sentence collected at the terminal. Nothing reclaims a body until it has been on disk for a day, because inside that window a body nothing references and a body whose row is still being written look alike. One process writes the data volume at a time. A command that has to write refuses while the server holds it and names the process that does, rather than decrypting a second copy and writing that back over whatever the server has recorded since. Stop the server for those. Nine reads are the exception and answer either way, off a read-only open: `account list` and `account show`, `domain list` and `domain show`, `dkim list` and `dkim records`, `blobs report`, `audit verify-chain` and `doctor`, which is exactly what you reach for while the server is up and behaving oddly. The entry on `blobs report` and `audit verify-chain` sets out what a read-only answer is bounded by. A read that is itself recorded is not among them: `audit read`, `account sieve` and `account messages` each take a reason and write the row saying somebody looked, so each needs the server stopped as a write does. The commands that read the outbound spool or a backup directory rather than the database are unaffected in either direction.

items.title: Outbound delivery, on one policy chain
items.body: Every outbound path composes the same chain rather than each growing its own: the receiver is resolved, MTA-STS is enforced against what its policy says, what the far side answered decides whether the message waits or stops, and a message that stops permanently produces a delivery report to the account that sent it. The budget is thirty five attempts, with waits of one minute, five, fifteen, an hour, and then four hours between every attempt after that, so a message is held for a little over five days before it is given up on and its sender told. That is the give-up time RFC 5321 section 4.5.4.1 asks for, and it is the scale a receiver plans its own maintenance against: a peer down for an afternoon gets its mail delivered on the other side of the outage rather than bounced. `BLAMEPOST_OUTBOUND_RETRY` changes it, and `maxAttempts` is the half to move, since past the fifth attempt each one adds four hours. A message that instead runs out of that budget against a fault no receiver ever owned, such as a policy record that never settled or an envelope the composer would not take, ends the same way and reports under `4.4.7`. A receiver whose name never resolved spends the same budget and reports `4.4.4`. Both are transient rather than permanent on purpose: no peer was ever reached, so nothing has been established about the address at all, and a sender reading either one knows the message is worth sending again where a permanent code would tell them it is not. The class is transient while the report's own action is `failed`, which is the pairing RFC 3464 §2.3.3 and §2.3.4 describe for a queue entry that expired. Nothing is discarded because a failure was not recognized. Whether a message keeps its place or ends is read from the outcome the chain returns, never from the words a peer chose, so a receiver cannot talk this server into abandoning mail by phrasing a refusal to look like something else. Reports are rate limited per sender and in total, twenty five an hour to any one sender and five hundred an hour altogether, because a report is addressed to whoever the failed message claimed to be from, and on a forged run that is somebody who never wrote to you. A third ceiling holds the table those per-sender counters live in to four thousand and ninety six senders at once, and past it a sender not already being tracked is refused a report as well. That one is spent by variety rather than by volume, so a backscatter flood or a server hosting many domains can reach it and leave a legitimate sender with no bounce at all, which is the one failure shape indistinguishable from delivery. All three are counted per process and a restart clears them, and `blamepost audit read --action blamepost.mail.delivery.report_unsent` names everyone who was owed a report and did not get one. DANE is composed and only enforced when you tell the server your resolver validates DNSSEC, since a server cannot discover that about its own resolver and asserting it falsely is worse than not running DANE at all. REQUIRETLS is not put on the wire, and the setting that asks for it refuses the boot rather than accepting a request no receiver will ever see.

items.title: The delivery reports this server receives about its own mail are read
items.body: A bounce for an account's message goes to that account, where a person reads it. Mail this server sends on its own behalf has nowhere to bounce that anybody checks: the TLS-RPT reports it owes the peers it delivers to go out from the postmaster address, and a report about one of them is the only signal that a reporting endpoint or an operator address has broken. The delivery reports it raises for accounts are not in that set, because RFC 5321 gives every such report an empty return path so one cannot start a run of reports about reports. What arrives for the postmaster is read and recorded, counted by the action each report states, and carried in the status the delivery layer reports about itself. No page or command renders those counts yet. Point BLAMEPOST_POSTMASTER at a real mailbox on a domain you host: the shipped default is built from the MX hostname, which is usually not a hosted domain, so a report addressed there is refused at the recipient and never arrives at all, and nothing else will tell you it is wrong. Nothing acts on a report, deliberately. Anyone can compose a well-formed report and send it to a postmaster address claiming any message failed, and acting on one would mean trusting a document a stranger wrote about mail you sent. There is nothing here that could prove the link either: no envelope identifier goes out, and a message a peer accepted and bounced afterwards left the outbound queue when it was accepted, so exactly the messages a report describes are the ones with no record left to match against. A report that cannot be read is recorded as unreadable rather than guessed at, with the reason kept, and ordinary mail to the postmaster is not counted as a failed report.

items.title: A message keeps the bytes it arrived with
items.body: Mail is not required to be valid UTF-8. RFC 6152 permits 8-bit content and legacy senders still produce it. A message carrying such bytes is stored and relayed exactly as it arrived, and the size reported for it, including the size a Sieve script tests against, is counted in octets rather than in characters. The two places that could quietly alter such a message both work in octets. The signature covers the bytes the sender wrote rather than a decoded copy, so what a receiver verifies is what left; hashing a decoded copy emits a signature that fails at every receiver, and returning one emits a signature over a message the sender never wrote. And it reads back byte for byte on every protocol: POP3 RETR and TOP, IMAP FETCH BODY[], and a partial fetch all return the stored octets, with the window a partial fetch takes measured in octets, which is what RFC 9051 section 6.4.5 counts in. What does leave a message unsigned has nothing to do with its character set: a domain this server holds no active selector for cannot be signed for, and that is recorded under an action of its own.

items.title: One stored copy of a shared message, and a delivery rewrites one that has gone short
items.body:
A message delivered to several accounts is stored once, named by the digest of its own content and sealed under the volume's key, so a mailing list message costs one copy on the volume rather than one per recipient. The account that arrives second files its row and reads the file already there.

That is also the one place a damaged body would spread. A file cut short by a restore that copied a prefix, by a write that stopped part way, or by a device that returned less than it was given is still a file at the right path, and every account handed the same message afterwards would inherit it and never have held a readable copy of its own. So a delivery compares the length of what is on disk against the message it is holding, and writes the message when the file is shorter than the sealed form of that message can be. It is the write that was about to happen anyway, and it lands atomically, so a repair cannot turn a short body into no body at all. Each one is recorded in the audit trail with the digest of the body it rewrote: a single repair is a bad sector, and a run of them is a volume to replace.

The length it compares against is a floor rather than an exact size, so read what it does not cover as carefully as what it does. It catches a large message cut below roughly three quarters of its length, a small one only when it is cut to a small fraction of it, and a body that changed without changing length not at all. Deciding any of those on every delivery would mean unsealing and re-hashing every message the volume already holds. Nothing is served for them either. IMAP and POP3 read the file, so they hash the stored octets back before returning them and refuse a body that does not hash to the digest naming it; the browser interface and JMAP render from the sealed row and never open the file at all. `blamepost blobs report --verify` names every file affected, and a body that will not open at all is refused in the same terms rather than reaching a client as a failure worth retrying.

items.title: The outbound queue has a bottom, and reaching it refuses mail rather than losing it
items.body: The queue shares one volume with the mailboxes, the message bodies and the audit trail, so it cannot be allowed to grow without a bound. Past its ceiling a submission is answered with a temporary code and the message stays in the sender's outbox, and an arriving message is answered the same way and stays with the peer that sent it, which is the party that can still do something about it. Mail arriving for forwarding stops short of the ceiling, at four fifths of it, so a flood aimed at an alias cannot spend the room your own accounts need in order to send. The delivery reports this server raises for senders stop at a tenth of it, which is the tightest of the three, so a queue that is filling does not also fill with notices about mail that already failed. Both a message count and a byte total apply, whichever is reached first, because depth is what every sweep pays and bytes are what the volume pays. queue flush claims each entry before attempting it, so two runs over one queue cannot attempt a message twice or move one out from under an attempt already in flight.

items.title: The health probes report whether mail is still moving
items.body: A queue that is filling and not draining reads from outside exactly like a healthy server: the ports are held, the store is open, the certificate is fresh, and mail is not leaving. Both probes carry a queue check, so a monitoring system finds that rather than the account holder whose message never arrived. It reduces the verdict from ok to degraded on three readings, and over the loopback interface it names which one fired; from anywhere else the answer is the verdict word alone. queue depth, or queue bytes, means the queue has filled past the point where it stops accepting mail for forwarding, which is not a warning level chosen for the probe but the reservation the queue already applies: reaching it means mail through an alias is being refused already and your own account holders are next. queue drain means mail is waiting and the sweep that retries it is not running. outbound transport means this build cannot put a message on the wire at all. Over the loopback interface the answer also carries how much is waiting, the depth at which forwarding stops, and how many messages the queue has refused since the server started. Neither probe refuses on any of them, so alert on degraded: a restart re-reads the same queue off the same volume and changes nothing about it, and withdrawing the interface takes away the console you would cancel the stuck mail from without moving any of the traffic that fills the queue. A queue that is stuck but small stays clean, deliberately, because a handful of messages retrying against one dead receiver is what an ordinary working server looks like; the operator guide says what to reach for instead when the question is about one destination rather than the whole queue.

items.title: TLS-RPT reports to the peers you deliver to
items.body: This server records how each delivery attempt's transport security went, for every domain it delivers to, and once a day it asks each of those domains where reports should go and submits an RFC 8460 aggregate report to the ones that answer. A domain that publishes no endpoint is sent nothing, and what that run judged for it is dropped rather than held. What is recorded is the successes and the failures that are genuinely about transport security; a refusal that has nothing to do with TLS, a full mailbox among them, is not recorded at all rather than counted as a broken handshake. Reports go where that domain's zone says at the moment of the run, and a destination the zone gives as a web address is posted to directly rather than composed as mail. One carries this server's hostname, the postmaster address as the contact a receiver replies to, the period it covers, the policy, the mail exchangers tried and the counts. No account address, no recipient, no subject and no message content is in one. blamepost does not yet read reports sent to your own endpoint; the operator guide says so plainly rather than leaving you publishing a record for nothing.

items.title: One container, one volume, no runtime dependencies
items.body: A two-stage build that runs as an unprivileged user, declares one data volume at /var/lib/blamepost, and is run by the compose file with every Linux capability dropped and no new privileges. NET_BIND_SERVICE is dropped with the rest, and 25, 143, 465, 587 and 4190 are still bound directly, because the compose file sets `net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start` to 0. That setting is namespaced to the container and changes nothing on the host. Host networking is the case it cannot serve, since the namespace is then the host's own: move each listener to a port above 1024 there and publish the standard one to it, and read what the operator guide says about the cost first, because a published port presents the mapping's address rather than the sender's and the per-address rate limits and the RBL checks are reading that address. Nothing the image is configured to run goes through a shell. The application resolves nothing from a package registry at run time or at image build time, because the framework it composes is vendored in the tree and ships inside the tarball. The compose file runs the same image and keeps optional content scanning and a TLS terminator behind profiles that are off unless you ask for them.

items.title: A renewed certificate reaches the running server without a restart
items.body: blamepost issues no certificate: BLAMEPOST_TLS_CERT and BLAMEPOST_TLS_KEY name two files your certificate client writes, and every sixty to ninety days it rewrites both of them underneath a server that is already running. Both files are watched. SMTP on 25, submission on 465 and 587, IMAP on 143, POP3 on 110 and ManageSieve on 4190 read the certificate as each connection arrives, so the first connection after the watcher picks the change up, which is within half a minute of the rewrite, is answered with the new one. Webmail, the administration surface and JMAP on 8443 pick it up as well: that port builds its own TLS context out of the two files, so it is handed the renewed pair when the reload happens rather than re-reading it per connection, and the next browser to connect gets the new certificate with the port never rebound and open connections never dropped. No port is left behind and no restart is part of a renewal. Each reload writes a line naming the certificate path it rebuilt from, whether it was the certificate or the key that changed, and any port still holding the old certificate. That last list is empty on this build, because every port named above takes the renewal. A renewal caught half written, with the certificate replaced and the key not yet, is discarded rather than installed, and the server keeps serving the pair it already had until a complete one appears.

items.title: A completed restore says what it has not opened
items.body: `blamepost restore apply` verifies the bundle's signature, puts the volume in place, opens it and walks its audit chain. None of that opens a message body. A backup preserves whatever state the volume was in when it was taken, so mail that was already unreadable comes back unreadable, and a backup taken while mail was arriving can carry a row whose body had not been written yet. The verb closes by sending you to `blamepost blobs report --verify`, which unseals every body a row names and hashes it back against that row, and then to `blamepost doctor` for the DKIM state a restore rewinds. Both are worth running before the server starts, and both answer while it holds the volume as well, from a read-only open whose rows stop at the last write to disk; each says how old that reading is before it reports anything. `doctor` counts bodies without opening one, so `blobs report --verify` is the only thing here that reads a message body at all. A restore onto a host with no data directory to move aside says so rather than naming a directory it kept.

items.title: Preservation orders are placed, read back and lifted from the command line
items.body: A court's order to keep records is answered with `blamepost account hold`, and every hard delete refuses those messages afterwards on IMAP, POP3, JMAP and webmail alike, an account erasure included. Finding the records comes first, so `blamepost account messages` lists what an account holds with the id each message is named by, the date it arrived here, the date the message shows, the sender and the subject, and marks anything already under an order; it never prints a body, and reading somebody's mail list takes a recorded reason the way reading their filter scripts does. `blamepost account holds` reads the orders back with the matter each cites, the custodian answerable for the records and who placed it, which is how you establish that an order is in force rather than trusting the command that placed it. An order names messages rather than a mailbox, so mail arriving afterwards is not swept into it silently, and it carries no expiry date, because nothing here sweeps one and a date recorded against an order would read as an end this server never acts on. `blamepost account release` lifts one and takes `--confirm` and an `--approver`, because the next expunge, POP3 commit, JMAP destroy or erasure on those messages will destroy them and an order is not lifted by whoever happens to be at the keyboard. Naming a message the account does not hold is refused by name and exits non-zero rather than reporting a duty that was never taken on. Placing and lifting each write a hash-chained row that `blamepost audit read` returns.

items.title: The installed package carries the documents it sends you to
items.body: `npm install @blamejs/blamepost` puts ROADMAP.md, THREAT-MODEL.md, ARCHITECTURE.md and LTS-CALENDAR.md on disk beside the README, along with the contributing, governance, support and conduct documents, so a link followed out of any page in the tarball resolves against a file that is there. Packing refuses a tarball in which any shipped document links to a file the tarball does not contain, so the set stays closed as documents are added.

items.title: `doctor` holds the sealed signing keys against the records that name them
items.body: `blamepost doctor` prints a `signing keys` line that reads the data directory's `keys` folder and the DKIM selector records together. It names the sealed private keys on the volume that no record claims, five of them by name and a count of any beyond that, which is signing material nothing on this server will use or remove and which every backup taken from then on carries, and it names every active selector whose key is not on the volume, which is a domain whose mail is leaving unsigned right now. A retiring selector with no key is neither and is not counted: retirement destroys the private half and keeps the record published through the overlap. Run while the server holds the volume, the records stop at its last write to disk while the keys folder is live, so a key written after that moment is counted apart as one the records had not reached rather than named as one nothing claims: an operator is never sent to destroy signing material their server is using.

items.title: `domain remove` reports the signing material it destroyed
items.body:
Withdrawing a domain prints the number of DKIM selector records and the number of sealed private keys it erased, and reminds you to pull the records from the zone yourself, because this server never edits DNS. `store.domains.remove` returns `keysErased` and `keysAlreadyGone` beside `selectorsRemoved`, and `store.domains.removeSelector` returns `keyErased`, so a caller can tell a key this call destroyed from one a retirement had already destroyed.

One outcome leaves you work, and it is printed rather than only counted. A sealed key that could not be destroyed after its records had already gone is named in the output, under the file name it is now sitting at, and comes back as `keysLeftAside`. Nothing on this server can find it again, because the record that named it is what is gone, so no second run of the command reaches it and the audit row for the withdrawal records a failure. Delete the file by hand: whoever holds one signs mail as that domain for as long as the volume and its backups last, including after somebody else takes the name on.

items.title: `UID SEARCH` answers in unique identifiers
items.body: IMAP clients may search with either spelling of the command. `SEARCH` answers in message sequence numbers and `UID SEARCH` answers in unique identifiers, as RFC 9051 §6.4.9 requires, and both are served by the same handler over the same keys, so a key one form refuses is refused by the other. One shape does not cross: a search term sent as an IMAP literal reaches the sequence-number spelling and not the identifier one, which answers `BAD` where the term should be. The search keys keep the meaning §6.4.4 gives them under both, so a bare sequence set is still a sequence set and a `UID` key is still identifiers. Apart from that one shape, only the answer changes. A client that keeps a cache between sessions asks for the identifier form because a sequence number means nothing outside the session that issued it, so this is the form that lets a mailbox be reopened without re-reading it.

items.title: `doctor` holds the spooled message bodies against the descriptors that name them
items.body: A message waiting for a retry is two files: the message itself, and the descriptor carrying the recipient, the attempt count and what the far side said. The ordinary listing reads descriptors, so a body whose descriptor is not there appears nowhere in it, while the queue's own ceiling is measured off the volume and weighs that body regardless: the room is spent with nothing in the ordinary listing to explain where it went. So both `blamepost queue list` and `blamepost doctor` account for those bodies separately, the first naming every one of them and the second naming five with a count of any beyond that, and `blamepost queue remove <id> --reason ...` acts on the id either one prints. A body written in the last five minutes is left out, because the pair is legitimately half on disk between the two writes and a message arriving normally must not be reported as one to delete.

items.title: `blobs report` and `audit verify-chain` answer while the server is running
items.body:
The two verbs you most want during an incident answer without the mail server being stopped first, from a read-only open of the same volume: the encrypted database is decrypted into a working copy that is never written back, the sealed database key is never re-sealed, no audit checkpoint is anchored, and the database handle refuses a write wherever one is issued. `doctor`, `account list`, `account show`, `domain list`, `domain show`, `dkim list` and `dkim records` take the same path, so nine verbs answer either way. Each prints how old the answer is before printing the answer, measured from the moment the server last wrote the volume to disk, and under `--json` that arrives inside an envelope so a script stops parsing rather than believing a stale answer.

`audit verify-chain` reaches the same verdict it reaches against a stopped server, signatures included. It walks the chain's own row hashes, verifies every checkpoint signature, and holds the record beside the volume against the rows, which is the combination a rewritten trail cannot satisfy: recomputing the hashes is cheap and forging a signature is not. What it covers is the chain up to the server's last write to disk, and the chain only ever grows, so that is a verified prefix rather than a partial reading.

`blobs report` reads two things that move at different speeds, and says so rather than guessing. The rows stop at the last write to disk while the blob directory is live, so a message delivered in between has its body on the volume and its row still in the server's own copy. That body is reported as one the rows had not reached, is not counted against the verdict, and is not reclaimable by anything. Everything else in the report is unaffected by how old the rows are: a row naming a body that is not on disk is missing whenever it is read, and `--verify`, which unseals every referenced body and hashes it back against the digest naming it, finds an altered body whenever it is read. `blamepost doctor` runs the same reader, so both reach a verdict on the message bodies and on the signing keys rather than reporting those two checks as not done.

items.title: `queue show` says what each attempt met, and how the message ends if nothing changes
items.body:
`blamepost queue show <id>` prints one queued message on its own: the recipient, the sender, when it was queued, its size, and then every attempt made on it, oldest first, with the host each attempt reached and what that receiver said in its own words. A listing carries one row per message and the last reason only, so two attempts refused for different reasons read there as a single refusal. Telling them apart is what separates a fault that moved from a fault that persists, and it is the question asked first when an account holder is waiting on a message.

The closing lines say where the message is headed: how much of its retry budget is spent, when the next attempt falls due, and who is told if the budget runs out. A message whose sender is the empty reverse path is itself a delivery report, so there is nobody to tell, and the line says so rather than naming an address that would not be written.

Take the id from `blamepost queue list`. An id this server did not mint is refused rather than turned into a path, and a well formed id with nothing behind it reports that the message is no longer waiting, which covers delivery, a message given up on, and a cancellation alike. `blamepost audit read --action blamepost.mail.queue.message_removed` says whether an operator removed it.

items.title: Mail between two accounts on this server is filed locally
items.body:
A message addressed to an account this server hosts is written into that account's mailbox, whether a mail client on 587 or 465 sent it, the compose form in the browser sent it, or a JMAP client called `EmailSubmission/set`. It does not depend on the MX record resolving, on the machine reaching its own public address, or on the MTA-STS and DANE policy the domain publishes about itself, and it takes no room in the outbound queue.

The local copy gets the delivery an arriving message gets: the recipient's Sieve script runs, the quota and the retention floor apply, and the filed copy carries the DKIM signatures the message was signed with. Aliases resolve first, so an address that forwards to a mailbox here is filed there and one that forwards off this server leaves over the outbound path. An envelope naming recipients here and elsewhere is split, and only the ones that leave count against the queue. An address this server hosts and cannot deliver to, such as a suspended mailbox, is reported to the sender rather than sent onward.

`docs/operator-guide.md` covers this under Mail between two mailboxes on this server.

items.title: The security posture is the boot sequence, not a set of flags
items.body:
Cross-site request forgery protection, origin and fetch-metadata checks, the bot guard, cookie prefixes, Trusted Types and encrypted sessions are wired into the request lifecycle, over a store whose sensitive columns are sealed at rest. There is no configuration that turns any of them off. The server additionally refuses to start when the vault, the at-rest encryption, the audit signing posture, the clock check, the Node version floor, the transport minimum, the data directory permissions, the runtime environment or an operator-installed certificate authority in the runtime trust store is not what a production deployment requires, and it names the predicate that refused.

One of those needs a firewall rule rather than a setting. Opening the store sends one SNTP query over UDP port 123 to a public time server, and a second to a fallback if the first does not answer, then compares the answer against this machine's clock, because the audit trail's timestamps are what an auditor reads and a host that has drifted writes a trail that is wrong without looking wrong. An hour or more of drift refuses the boot and names the number. Five minutes or more writes a warning and the boot continues, and anything under that writes an ordinary line naming the drift. No answer at all writes a warning too, `ntp warning: NTP unreachable`, and the boot goes on with the clock unchecked. That line suggests BLAMEJS_NTP_STRICT=1, which is already the default and governs measured drift rather than an unanswered query, so the fix is to open UDP 123 outbound or to point BLAMEJS_NTP_SERVERS at a time source you run. BLAMEJS_SKIP_NTP_CHECK=1 drops the query and the warning with it. None of the three is a substitute for the host synchronizing its own clock; this runs once, at boot.

items.title: Post-quantum first, with classical algorithms beside rather than instead
items.body: Where the choice is this project's to make, the key encapsulation is an ML-KEM-1024 and P-384 hybrid, the audit checkpoints are signed with SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f, digests and key derivation are SHA3-512 and SHAKE256, passwords are hashed with Argon2id, and everything sealed on the volume is encrypted with XChaCha20-Poly1305. Release artifacts carry an ML-DSA-65 sidecar signature from the first release cut after the signing key is set up, which the entry on verifying a release covers. Where an interoperable wire format settles the algorithm instead, it does not, and DKIM is the case worth knowing about. The DKIM-Signature a= tag draws from an IANA registry that has no post-quantum value, so outbound mail is signed with both an Ed25519 and an RSA selector and a receiver that has not implemented RFC 8463 still gets an authenticated message. Both of those are classical, and nothing post-quantum stands beside them until a key type is registered. The transport key exchange is a different shape: every listener names the set it accepts, leads it with post-quantum hybrids and asks a peer that implements one to use it, which the entry on those listeners covers. What relays unsigned rather than altered is a message the signer refused: a domain holding no active selector or only half a pair, a key file that cannot be read, one carrying no seal, and one the vault will not open. Each leaves a row carrying the code that says which.

items.title: A hosted domain signs with both DKIM algorithms or with neither, never with one
items.body: Ed25519 and RSA-SHA256 are the two algorithms a DKIM signature can name, and a hosted domain that signs at all publishes one selector of each. `blamepost domain add` and `blamepost init` mint the pair as they take the domain on; a domain added from the administration interface is hosted before it holds any key, and its mail leaves unsigned until you mint one there. There is no setting that turns one of them off and no verb an operator can reach withdraws half a pair: retiring names a pair and takes both halves, so a domain cannot be left signing with one algorithm. If a receiver mishandles the second signature header, publish both records anyway. RFC 6376 requires a verifier to ignore a signature whose algorithm it does not implement (section 3.3.4) and says it should keep checking the rest (section 6.1), and a receiver that cannot do that will also mishandle mail from any sender part way through a key rotation. A domain that does hold one algorithm, which a mint or a retirement interrupted part way can leave behind, signs nothing until it holds both again, and the refusal says which half is missing. The way back from either half is to retire what is left and mint a fresh pair, with the domain unsigned between those two steps. Retirement is named by the Ed25519 selector and looks for the RSA half under that name with `-rsa` on the end, which is how every pair is minted, so a domain left holding only its RSA half is retired by naming the Ed25519 selector that half was minted beside: the surviving name with `-rsa` taken off it. `blamepost dkim list` prints what is left, and a name that matches nothing is refused with the selectors the domain does hold.

items.title: This server does not relay for an address range, and says so at start rather than later
items.body: Granting relay to a range of source addresses stops the boot, naming the setting and what to do instead. The reason is worth knowing before you reach for it elsewhere: every mail listener here requires TLS before it will accept an envelope, so a device that gets as far as naming a recipient on port 25 has already completed a handshake, and a device that can do that can authenticate on the submission port. The only device an address range could have served that an account cannot is one with no encryption at all, and that device is answered `530 5.7.0 Must issue a STARTTLS command first` at `MAIL FROM`, before it has named a recipient. The range carried the whole risk of relaying for anything else on that network and bought nothing. Give the printer or the application server an account. A range names a segment rather than a party, so when one machine on it is compromised the only lever is withdrawing the range and taking the printer down with it, while an account is suspended on its own and has a mailbox where a delivery failure can be read.

items.title: The certificate is read before anything binds, and doctor reads it too
items.body: A certificate that has expired is a file that is still present and still readable, so a server that checked only for a file would start, take every port, and refuse every connection offered to it, while reporting itself healthy. The pair is opened before the first listener binds. A certificate whose validity has closed or has not opened yet, a key that belongs to a different certificate, a file that is not a certificate at all, a key the vault will not unseal, and either file the process cannot read each stop the start and name both paths and the reason. Two of those are what a first boot meets. This image drops privileges, so a key left readable only by root is a key it cannot read; and a certificate reported as not valid until a date ahead of now is usually a host whose clock is wrong rather than a certificate to reissue. `blamepost doctor` reports the same reading without starting anything: the expiry date and the days left, whether the key matches, whether the certificate covers the name this server announces, and whether the file holds the full chain or only the leaf. That last one is the mistake that survives testing, because a browser fetches a missing issuer itself and a sending mail server does not, so a leaf-only certificate passes a check in your browser and stops your mail. A certificate that is wrong but still usable is reported and logged and does not stop the server, because every peer that does not check the thing it got wrong is served exactly as before. The private key is opened only to compare it against the certificate, and never appears in a report or a log line.

items.title: The health probes read the certificate, so a renewal that stopped running is found before mail stops
items.body: A renewal client that dies is the slowest outage this server has. Nothing changes for weeks, and then every peer stops talking to it at once. Nothing else either probe reads moves while it happens: the listeners stay bound and the store stays open for the whole of it. So `/healthz` and `/readyz` carry a `certificate` check that reads the pair on disk on every poll rather than once at boot, since a reading taken at boot describes the certificate the renewal replaced. The verdict drops from `ok` to `degraded` as soon as the certificate is inside a fortnight of expiring, the chain is incomplete, the name this server announces is not covered, or the two files no longer agree. Over the loopback interface, which is where the container's own health check runs, the answer also carries the days remaining, a flag saying whether the pair is one this server could present at all, and the names of the readings that failed. Alert on `degraded`. The probe reduces its verdict and never refuses, including for a certificate that has already run out, and that is deliberate: refusing would take a server out of rotation while it is still carrying mail for every peer, withdraw the interface you would have read the reason from, and invite a restart that this server would refuse to complete, since it does not start on a certificate it cannot present. Renew the certificate and the running server picks it up on every port it binds, with no restart.

items.title: A protection this server cannot apply refuses at start rather than reporting itself
items.body: Asking every outbound envelope for REQUIRETLS stops the boot, naming the setting and the protections that do apply instead. RFC 8689 lets a sender tell a receiver to hold a message back rather than deliver it over a connection it could not encrypt, and this server cannot make that request: the flag is carried as far as the transport, and the transport does not put the parameter on the wire, so no receiver is ever asked. Refusing rather than ignoring is the point. A setting that grants something and cannot deliver fails in the open, and somebody notices on the first attempt. A setting that protects something and cannot deliver fails quietly and in your favor: mail keeps flowing, nothing bounces, no delivery report says anything is wrong, and the evidence that confidential mail is being withheld from peers that cannot encrypt is identical to the evidence that it was never asked for. An operator who trusted the flag would have no way to find out. Transport security on the way out is enforced by MTA-STS, which applies to every outbound message and refuses a peer whose certificate does not match its published policy, and by DANE once you have told the server that its resolver validates DNSSEC. That last condition is not a formality and DANE does nothing without it: the standard forbids acting on a TLSA record that was not validated, and no server can discover that fact about the resolver it was pointed at. Know what neither of them reaches. Against a receiving domain that publishes no MTA-STS policy and no TLSA record, the mail exchanger this server connects to is named by a DNS answer nothing validated, and a host holding a valid certificate for a name of its own satisfies every check that is left. The connection is encrypted, and it may be encrypted to somebody else. What closes that is the receiving domain publishing one of the two, which is not yours to publish for them. Leaving the setting unset, or writing it down as off, starts the server normally.

items.title: The cross-site gate stands down only for a caller with no ambient credential, and never stands the origin check down
items.body: A state change arriving at the browser surface is held to a double submit token and to an origin cross-check, and the one waiver either of them has is narrow and deliberate. It applies to a caller that sends no cookie at all, and to nothing else. Such a caller has no ambient credential for a page on another site to spend, which is the whole of what this class of attack is, and it carries no token back, so demanding one would be an outage on the JMAP bearer path rather than a defense. A request that sends a cookie is validated whatever else it carries. An authorization header buys nothing: a header is something the party composing the request writes, so its presence is evidence of nothing, and this server resolves a session from the cookie before it reads one anyway, which means a request carrying both is authenticated by exactly the credential the gate exists to protect. The origin cross-check is never waived, by that caller or any other. It answers a different question than the token compare does, and there is no reading of a request being cookieless under which a cross-origin state change becomes acceptable, so a bearer client asking for one from another site is refused like anybody else. What this means in practice: a token-only client works with no token to send, a browser session is checked on every state change, and neither one can be talked out of the origin check by anything it puts in a header.

items.title: A mailbox reused for a new account tells clients to forget what they cached
items.body: Every IMAP folder carries a number that tells a client whether the identifiers it remembers still mean the same messages, and the standard requires that number never to go backwards or repeat. Taken from the clock alone, deleting an account and creating the same address again within the same second would produce that number twice while the message identifiers underneath restarted from one, and a client holding a cache from before would keep it and map what it remembered onto whatever now holds those identifiers, which after a re-provisioning is somebody else's mail. So it comes from the clock only when that is higher than anything the volume has ever issued, so it climbs across a re-provisioning, across a restore from backup, and across a clock correction while the server runs, and it refuses rather than wrapping if it ever reaches the ceiling the format allows.

items.title: Correcting the server's clock costs no mail and hands back no spent budget
items.body: Several rules here are windows rather than states, and a window measured against the wall clock moves when an operator fixes the time or a time service steps it. Three of them would. A POP3 session holds its mailbox exclusively while it is open, and timed on the wall clock a correction forward past the timeout would hand the mailbox to somebody else while the first session still had it. That is worse than it sounds, because the protocol only applies deletions when a session ends cleanly, so the marks that session had made would go with it and the account holder would watch deleted mail come back. A correction backwards has the mirror problem: an abandoned session's lock could not expire until the clock caught up. The bound on how many delivery reports this server will send in an hour would reset on a step as well, handing back the whole allowance without any time having passed, which matters because that bound exists to stop a forged run turning this server into somebody else's flood. And a transport report could claim a period that ended before it began. So the first two measure elapsed time from a source an operator cannot move, and so do the three budgets behind a sign in: the one kept against a mailbox, the smaller one kept against a single machine, and the thirty days a machine stays familiar to a mailbox it has signed in from. A step in either direction ends none of those early or late. The third stays a wall-clock instant, because RFC 8460 puts it in front of a receiver as a real date and files the report under it, so a start later than the present is re-anchored to now rather than withheld: the counts underneath it are observations the receiver is owed, and letting a clock correction suppress them would be the same failure in other clothes. What deliberately uses the calendar is the outbound retry schedule, because a message waiting to be retried has to survive a restart and an elapsed count does not. Two budgets are still counted against the wall clock, and both are ceilings rather than mail: the authentication failures each listener counts against one source address over a quarter of an hour, and the five minute window in front of the browser sign in form. A correction forward can end either of those early.

items.title: A listener held back on purpose is not reported as one that failed
items.body: A listener has four states rather than two, and only one of them is a fault. It took its port, or the configuration did not turn it on, or it is enabled and deliberately held back with the server's own sentence saying why, or it was enabled and expected to bind and did not. Only the last is a failure. This matters most on the very first boot, which every operator passes through: port 25 holds itself back while no domain is hosted, because a server accepting mail for recipients it knows nothing about is collecting a stranger's mail. Reporting that as a port that failed to bind would make a fresh container read as unhealthy for the whole window between coming up and being configured, while submission, mailbox access and the browser interface were all bound and serving. Anything acting on that reading would treat the server as broken, and an orchestrator watching liveness would restart it in a loop, which fixes none of the causes and takes down the interface the operator was about to finish setup in. So liveness answers degraded rather than failing: the process is worth keeping and something is held back, said in one answer. Readiness is what refuses when a listener was expected to bind and did not, because stopping traffic is the response that fits; a listener held back on purpose reduces readiness to degraded rather than failing it, for the same reason liveness does. A store that will not open fails both, since that is the one condition a restart can address. The health probe writes its verdict, so a container runtime carries the reason beside the failing streak instead of an empty string, and the same distinction reaches the console: starting the server lists what bound and what is being held back with the sentence saying why, rather than leaving an absence to carry the answer.

items.title: Withdrawing a domain stops its mail at the next message rather than the next restart
items.body: Disabling or removing a hosted domain changes the answer port 25 gives, immediately, with no restart in between. Peers are refused permanently at the recipient, so a sender reports the failure to whoever wrote the message instead of retrying for days against a decision you meant to make. A recipient at a domain the listener started with is measured again against the hosted set as it stands at that moment rather than against the set the listener started with, which is what keeps the wire agreeing with what every management surface says about the domain. Switching a domain back on is live in the same way, provided it was hosted when the server started; a domain that was already switched off at that point needs the restart an added domain needs. That restart is the safe direction: a domain you ADD is refused until the server is restarted, which the setup sequence already requires because the acknowledgment gate is read at startup too. Publish the MX record after that restart rather than before, so the gap is not mail that bounces. A stranger refused this way is told only that this server does not handle mail for that domain, never which of the two happened or that it was once hosted here; that distinction is kept in the audit trail, where the operator can read it and the sender cannot.

items.title: A name server that goes quiet cannot hold anything open, and never passes for an answer
items.body: Inbound authentication asks the resolver questions while a peer waits: the reverse name of the connecting address, the sending domain's policy records. A resolver that accepts a question and never answers is a different failure from one that refuses, and left unbounded it would stop the session outright, holding it until the idle timeout with the peer told nothing and the connection counted against the ceiling the whole time. So those lookups carry their own deadline of forty-five seconds, and a peer that outlives it gets a temporary refusal it can retry. That is set well above anything a working resolver needs, since the resolver this server builds already bounds each of its own upstream fetches at ten seconds, so it never fires in ordinary operation. One thing it deliberately does not do is treat running out of time as an answer: a lookup that never came back is never read as a record that is not published, because that would let anyone silence a policy by stalling its query rather than by having to break it. The posture check reads the same way. `blamepost doctor` bounds every lookup it makes, so a stalled resolver cannot hold a report open with nothing on screen, and a record it could not get an answer about is reported as a third outcome rather than as a missing one. The admin view resolves nothing itself: the posture column there is the acknowledgment you recorded, and the page sends you to `blamepost doctor` for what is actually published. That distinction is the useful part: a record reported missing sends you to edit a zone that may well be correct and published, while a record reported unchecked sends you to the resolver this server reads, which is where the problem actually is. An unchecked record names neither what was expected nor what was found, because neither was observed, and a run that could not settle a record this server requires does not report itself as passing. An advisory record nobody could get an answer about is said in the summary and leaves the exit status alone, so a monitor watching the status alone should read the report rather than the number.

items.title: A body that reads as two messages is refused at the wire and again before delivery
items.body: Servers do not all agree on what ends a message, and that disagreement is how one submitted message becomes two at the receiver, the second carrying a sender nobody authenticated and inheriting the authentication of the first. Each SMTP listener refuses the shape at the point of parse, and the assembled body is measured once more at each of the two handoffs a message from the wire crosses on its way to delivery, the inbound one on port 25 and the relay one on submission. A message composed in the browser or over JMAP reaches neither handoff and cannot carry the shape in any case: the composer rewrites every bare line ending to CRLF and encodes any line that begins with a period, so there is nothing there to find. The submission listener advertises `CHUNKING`, so both spellings are reachable there and the screen runs on the chunked `BDAT` path as well as the line-by-line `DATA` one. A `BDAT` payload is an opaque byte stream under RFC 3030 §3, so it is not dot-unstuffed, and the screen applies to it anyway: the body is relayed onward and the next hop is usually `DATA`, where a bare line feed is what lets one message be read as two. A well-formed chunked message is unaffected, and a body refused when sent whole is refused when sent in chunks. A refused one is recorded under its own audit action and reaches neither a mailbox nor the spool.

items.title: An operator can see who is locked out and let them back in
items.body: A run of wrong passwords against one mailbox closes it to further attempts, which is the point, and it also means an account holder can be locked out by somebody else's guessing. A machine that mailbox has signed in from successfully within the last thirty days is let through anyway, unless that machine has spent the smaller budget kept against it, so a guessing run usually reaches the owner's newest device rather than the one they use every day. That exemption is held in the running process, so a restart drops it and the owner is then refused everywhere until the budget decays or you release it. The administration interface shows what has been locked, which budget did it, from which machine, and when it lifts on its own, and lets you release it with a recorded reason. Naming the machine matters and the page says so: the per-machine budget is read before the per-mailbox one, so releasing only the mailbox leaves the client that spent its own allowance still refused, which is the shape where an operator reports success and the account holder still cannot read mail on their phone. A machine this server cannot read as an address at all refuses the whole release rather than doing half of it, so nothing is released, the mailbox included. Refusing is the kinder answer: the table of real keys is on the same page as the form, so the cost is retyping one field, against a release that reports success while leaving untouched the very budget you were clearing. What did happen is read rather than inferred, because the notice names which budgets were released and which were left alone, and a machine you named whose budget was already clear reads differently from a machine you never named. The two mixed answers are the useful ones, and neither could be expressed while this was a single yes or no: a named machine that was already clear rules that device out and sends you to look elsewhere, while a mailbox that was already clear says the machine was the only thing refusing, which is why releasing the mailbox on its own had not helped. Each listener that authenticates also counts failures per source address on its own, and nothing releases that. The count is kept over a rolling quarter of an hour, so the refusal lifts once enough of the earliest failures have aged past that window rather than a quarter of an hour after the last one, and a source already at the ceiling records no further failures to push it out. The browser sign-in holds a bound of its own shape, counting every attempt from one address over five minutes rather than only the failures, and nothing on this page releases that one either. So a release that reports success has cleared the two budgets it names and nothing else, which is what the notice is careful to say.

items.title: Authentication failures are budgeted per identity, not only per address
items.body: An attacker rotating source addresses against one known mailbox is bounded, on the browser sign-in and on submission, IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve alike, and the budget is shared across them so a lockout spent on one protocol is not refilled by moving to another. Passwords are hashed with Argon2id and checked against a bundled common-password list when one is set. The browser's sign-in form carries a second bound of its own, on work rather than on guessing: fifty posts in five minutes from one source address. This server reads the peer off the socket and ignores X-Forwarded-For, so with a TLS terminator in front of the browser port every reader arrives from the terminator's address and those fifty posts are one count for the whole server.

items.title: Changing a password takes effect against a sign in already under way
items.body: Signing in with a stored hash below the current Argon2id parameters replaces it, so raising the cost reaches every account as its owner signs in rather than needing a reset for each one. Argon2id is slow on purpose, which makes that replacement a long gap with the account row already read. So the stored hash is read again before the replacement is written, and the write is abandoned when it no longer matches what the sign in was working from. That is the case where it matters. Containing a credential that has been taken means changing the password, and a sign in already under way with the old one would otherwise finish by writing the old password's hash back over the new one: the change would report success, you would have confirmation you had made it, and the credential you were containing would still open the mailbox on submission, IMAP, POP3, ManageSieve and the browser. Abandoning the replacement costs nothing and never fails the sign in, because the credential it presented was correct when it presented it and the replacement is a saving on top of that answer rather than part of it.

items.title: The ARC chain is evaluated and reported, and deliberately changes nothing
items.body: A message carrying an authentication chain from an intermediary has that chain evaluated beside SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and the result is written into the Authentication-Results header your clients and filters read: none when there is no chain, pass when every seal verifies, fail when they do not. RFC 8617 gives the chain those three tokens and no more, so fail covers a seal that was checked and rejected and a sealer's key that could not be looked up alike; the mail.server.mx.envelope_verdict audit row separates the two, which is what stops a run of resolver failures reading as a run of forgeries. It moves no message. A chain is worth exactly what the party that sealed it is worth, and there is no setting here that names the intermediaries you vouch for, so a chain that validates cannot lift a DMARC failure and a broken one cannot cause a refusal. Anyone who can register a domain can seal a flawless chain over their own forgery claiming somebody else's domain passed, which is why acting on one without knowing who sealed it would be worse than not looking at all. A recipient's own Sieve script can read the result and file on it, and an account holder who subscribes to a mailing list is better placed to know they trust it than this server is.

items.title: One account cannot reach another account's folders
items.body: There is one folder namespacing scheme, and every read and every mutation an account drives resolves the acting account before it touches a folder. That layer is the only place isolation can happen: the message store underneath keeps a flat namespace of folders with no owner column, so a surface that listed folders without asking the layer that records ownership would list the whole server's. A verb that cannot identify its account refuses rather than falling back to a shared folder, on IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve as well as in the browser and over JMAP, so no account reaches another's mail, folders or message identifiers.

items.title: Deleting an account defaults to archiving it, and erasing one reaches its mail
items.body: Destroying an account takes an explicit flag and a recorded reason, which is the deliberate act GDPR Article 17 asks for rather than the default meaning of a delete. An erasure reaches the aliases pointing at it, its mailboxes, its messages, its filter scripts, its annotations and every sealed message body no message left on this server still names, and it takes the account row last, once nothing it holds is left to name it. It runs through the same delete path IMAP EXPUNGE takes. It also reaches mail the message store still holds that no mailbox row names, which is what a delivery interrupted between its two writes leaves and which no protocol lists: those messages meet the same order and the same floor as the rest, and the audit row `blamepost.mail.mailbox.account_mail_erased` counts them apart under `messagesUnfiledErased` and `messagesUnfiledKept`, since that row is the only place an operator can account for them. So a message under a preservation order, or inside the retention floor a compliance posture sets, stays: `blamepost account remove --destroy` names each one with the mailbox it is in and the reason it stayed, keeps that mailbox so the message is still addressable, and exits non-zero only when something could not be erased for another reason. What an erasure does not reach is a backup or a snapshot taken before it ran, because a message body is sealed under the volume's key rather than under anything the erasure destroys, so set the expiry of your backups against the erasure requests you expect to answer.

items.title: An erasure destroys the mail first and the identity last, so nothing it keeps is stranded
items.body:
An erasure is partial whenever a preservation order or the retention floor keeps a message, and that is the system working: GDPR Article 17(3)(e) is the exception you answer the request with. A record you are required to produce has to stay producible, though, and every surface that could produce one resolves the account it belongs to first. So the mail goes first and the account row goes last, only once nothing still names it: no mailbox row, no filter script, no annotation and no alias.
