That is judged by reading the rows back rather than by what the delete path answered, and it counts everything the account holds rather than its mailboxes alone, because a filter script a governance gate held back is as unreachable as a kept message once the identity is gone.

When something is held back the account is kept and reported as kept: `blamepost account remove --destroy` opens with `Partly erased` rather than `Erased`, names each message and the rule keeping it, and says the account row was kept and why. That account is out of service from the moment the erasure runs. It refuses every credential on every listener and in the browser, and `blamepost account resume` refuses it, because the mail it held is already destroyed and nothing brings that back. It takes no delivery either: a peer naming that address at `RCPT TO` is answered `550 5.1.1` with the same sentence an address this server never held gets, before a byte of the message body is transmitted. That is permanent where the other two ways a mailbox is held are temporary, and deliberately so. A suspension and a disabled domain are lifted by the operator, so a sender should keep the message and try again; this state is not lifted, the row leaves only when the erasure finishes, and after that the address is answered `5.1.1` anyway. A temporary answer would spend the whole of the sending server's retry window against an address that can never accept the message and then return it to the person who wrote it days later, describing a condition that was never transient. It shows in `blamepost account list` as `erasing` without being asked for, so an unfinished erasure is visible rather than reading as a finished one, and running the same command again once the order is lifted or the window has passed erases what was held back and takes the row with it.

Two records say an erasure is outstanding, and the status column is only one of them. The account row carries `erasureHeldAt` beside its status, and the erasure files a chain entry of its own as it closes; the verbs that could otherwise return an account to service read both. That second record is what closes a gap the first cannot. Writing the status is one write and a volume can refuse it, because a records-retention posture puts a trigger on that column and refuses the transition itself, so the marker is attempted on its own when the transition will not land, and where neither lands the trail still answers. An account whose mark went nowhere would otherwise read as being in service with its mail already destroyed, and could be archived and then reinstated straight back into ordinary use. Whichever record is present the account reads as `erasing` and stays out of service, and archiving one is refused for the same reason reinstating it is: it would put a row whose mail is gone back within reach of reinstatement and close an erasure this server still owes.

The last two writes are answered for on the same terms as everything before them. A gate can refuse the erase of the account row itself, which leaves the account exactly where a kept filter script leaves it; the write putting the account out of service is attempted twice, once as the whole status change and once as the erasure marker on its own, and only a volume that refuses both prints `FAIL`, because then the mail is gone and the mailbox is still authenticating until you suspend it. Neither raises: by that point the mail is destroyed, and an exception in place of the report would leave nothing anywhere saying so.

Know what an order covers before you rely on it: it is placed on a message and covers the message it names, which the entry on preservation orders sets out along with what to reach for where a matter needs more than that. `blamepost blobs report` agrees with all of this: it lists mail no account holds, and mail an order or the floor is keeping does not appear there, because its account is still on the table holding it.

items.title: Signing keys leave a trail, and it names both sides of a rotation
items.body: Minting a selector, rotating one, retiring one and sweeping one out early are all recorded, and so is an attempt the signer refused: a key already active, a selector name already taken, or a selector this domain does not hold. Those are recorded because the refusal changes nothing on the volume and would otherwise leave no trace at all. An invocation turned away for a domain this server does not host, or for a name it cannot read as a domain, is answered at the terminal and not written down. An argument the signer itself refuses, a selector that is not a DNS label or a retirement naming none, is recorded like any other refusal. A rotation names the selector leaving and the selector arriving in the same row, because the question an incident asks is which key was live when a given message was signed, and that pairing exists nowhere else: the individual selector records show each half of the arriving pair being added, and each half of the outgoing pair being withdrawn when it is retired, with nothing tying the two sets together. What a row never carries is key material of either half, or any digest of it. A published key confirms a guessed private half offline without a request ever reaching this server, and nothing running here takes a value back out of the trail once it is written: only an operator archiving a range and purging it removes rows, and that is a separate act that asks before it runs. A row names a selector and an algorithm, which is what a receiver already reads off any signature this server sends.

items.title: The audit trail and the stored bodies are each checked against something outside themselves
items.body: A hash-linked chain proves that it agrees with itself, which is a weaker thing than proving nothing changed: anyone who can rewrite a row can recompute every hash that follows it. Append-only triggers stop that through this server's own database handle, and they stop nothing for somebody reaching the decrypted file outside it, where the signed checkpoints can be deleted rather than forged. So the volume keeps a separate record of where the chain stood when it was last anchored, and refuses to open when the rows disagree with that record. That record is held against the row it names in both directions: a row that hashes differently is a rewrite, and a row that is simply gone is a deletion unless an unsigned purge record in the database claims the range, which is the one thing that legitimately leaves a gap and the one thing here that nothing verifies: that case is reported as a gap the run did not read rather than as one accounted for. A stored message body is checked the same way, against the digest that names its file, on every retrieval that opens the file rather than only when a reporting command happens to run. That is IMAP `FETCH` and `BODY[]`, and POP3 `RETR` and `TOP`. Webmail and JMAP render from columns inside the encrypted, authenticated database and never open the file at all, so the rename this defends against does not reach them. Sealing proves this server wrote a body. It does not prove the body is the one the row asked for, and the distance between those two statements is a single file rename.

items.title: A finding against the audit trail survives being read, and the volume stays shut until you clear it
items.body: Opening the volume anchors the chain again, which replaces the record the rows were about to be held against. So the one refusal that catches a trail rewritten in full, with its signed checkpoints deleted rather than forged, could only ever fire once: running the command a second time to be sure would have reported the volume intact. So the finding is written to audit.disputed in the data directory before the refusal is raised, and every later open reads it and refuses under the same code rather than appending to a trail nobody can stand behind. The one open that does not write it is the read-only one a reporting verb takes, which withholds the re-anchor too, so the finding is reported there and recorded by the next open that can write. Removing that file is the operator's decision and nothing does it for them. The refusals reach `blamepost audit verify-chain` as verdicts, with `--json` output a monitor can alert on, rather than as a command that crashed.

items.title: The audit trail says what it proved, and never reports a check it could not make
items.body: `blamepost audit verify-chain` reports three readings on their own lines: the chain math, the signed checkpoints, and the record beside the database. It says which of the three it made rather than reporting that nothing was inserted, altered or removed whenever the first two pass: a volume with no readable record beside it is told the rows were held against nothing outside the database they live in, which is what a volume on its first run looks like. The passing verdict is scoped to what it can actually prove: the key signing the checkpoints is sealed under the same passphrase that decrypts the database, so the guarantee is that no row was inserted, altered or removed by anyone who did not hold that passphrase. SECURITY.md, THREAT-MODEL.md and the operator guide say the same thing, and the operator guide's incident-response section explains how to tell storage damage from a rewrite and what each one calls for.

items.title: A purged range is reported as a range this server did not read
items.body:
An archive and purge deletes audit rows on purpose, and where the deletion stopped is recorded in a table inside the database. That table is the weakest thing on the volume: no signature over it, no link into the hash chain, no checkpoint covering it and no append-only trigger guarding it, so a process that can write to the open database can put a row there without touching a signature, while rewriting the rows or forging a checkpoint has to get past the append-only triggers or hold the vault passphrase. One row there discards every audit row at or below the counter it names.

So `blamepost audit verify-chain` never reports a volume carrying one as a trail nothing was removed from. It reports `note a gap this run did not read, trusted on an unsigned counter`, names the counter, and says plainly that no archive was verified, because nothing here verifies one: the identifier the record carries names the signed checkpoint the archive was made against rather than a location, and the archive bundle is a directory you were told to keep where this server cannot reach it. Moving a bundle off the volume is expected and changes nothing about the check. What the command can resolve is whether that checkpoint is still on the volume at or above the purged range, and it says which; a rewrite that deleted rows and relinked the survivors has to delete the checkpoints over them, so one still standing means the surviving rows were not relinked, and means nothing about the rows that are gone.

The note survives being read. Any command that opens the volume anchors the chain again over a row that is still there, so the comparison that found the gap cannot make itself twice, and a second run would otherwise report an ordinary volume. The finding is recorded in audit.disputed and repeated on every later run until you remove it. Unlike the findings recorded there for a rewritten trail, it does not shut the volume: this is a range nothing established in either direction, and refusing to deliver mail over it would be the wrong trade. To close it, read the archive bundle for the range back with `blamepost audit verify-bundle` and hold its counters against the counter in the note. If no bundle covers the range, those rows were removed rather than archived. Reading a bundle back whose covering signature could not be checked says so in the first line of the answer rather than only in the detail below it.

items.title: The audit trail is anchored while the server runs, and again when it stops
items.body:
The record beside the database is what a wholesale rewrite of the chain has to get past: a rewritten trail agrees with itself, and the signed checkpoints over it can be deleted rather than forged, so the counter and hash recorded outside the database are the witness left. That record advances only when a checkpoint is written. Opening the volume writes one, a running server writes one an hour, and a stop writes a last one: `blamepost serve` flushes the buffered rows, anchors the chain and flushes again as an ordered shutdown phase before the store closes, so a cleanly stopped volume is anchored at its newest row and the events the shutdown itself produced are on disk rather than lost with the process.

What that leaves is the hour before a server that is killed rather than stopped, and it is worth planning for. An out of memory kill, a host reboot, a container killed rather than signaled and a power loss all end the process without a stop, and the rows written since the last hourly anchor are then covered by the chain and the checkpoints alone. Give your supervisor a stop timeout longer than the shutdown takes, so the usual case closes the window instead of bounding it. The hour is not an operator setting: no BLAMEPOST_ variable and no configuration key reaches it, and the only lever is a validated, bounded argument to `blamepost.create`, which means embedding this server rather than running the image. It is priced that way because each anchor stores a signature of about fifty kilobytes on the volume permanently and adds a few milliseconds to every later `blamepost audit verify-chain`, so a shorter interval buys a smaller window at a cost that grows for as long as the server runs. An hour in which nothing was recorded costs nothing, because there is no new tip to sign.

items.title: A refusal tells the account holder what went wrong, not where this server keeps things
items.body:
When a client asks for a message whose stored body is not on the volume, the refusal identifies it by the first sixteen characters of that body's content digest, and points at the command that reports how much of the store is affected. That is not the object id, the IMAP UID or the Message-ID, and the reply carries neither the absolute path the body would have had nor the digest in full. An ordinary account holder reaches this refusal on a plain retrieval, so anything it carried would describe the data directory's layout on disk to somebody entitled to their own mail alone. The path is nowhere in the reply, and the digest is cut to enough characters to match a message against a report and not enough to be one.

How far that match carries depends on which fault it is. `blamepost blobs report --verify` prints a body that does not match its digest under the same sixteen characters, so those line up directly. It prints a body that is missing by object id and UID with no digest at all, and missing is the fault this refusal usually reports, so hold the two together under `--json`, where the missing entry carries the digest in full. The fuller answer an operator needs is not on the wire in either case, which is why the refusal names that command. A body that does not match its digest is refused in its own terms rather than folded into the missing case, because that one means bytes changed under a file nothing rewrites.

The administration surface holds to the same line. A selector change that the signer refuses is shown to you word for word, because the signer writes those refusals for a person and they say what is already published and what to do instead. A selector change that failed for some other reason is not: a data volume that cannot be written raises a message carrying the directory the sealed private keys live in, the scheme their filenames are built from and the suffix an atomic write appends to its temporary file. That goes to the log, where a fault belongs, and the page says the change was not made and points you at it.

Which refusals count as the signer's is decided by the list of them it publishes rather than by the family its error codes belong to, because the framework underneath shares that family and writes its own faults for whoever composed it, in vocabulary naming internal functions and arguments you cannot pass. So the page shows you what the signer said about your domain and your selector, and everything else reaches the log instead.

items.title: A trail that cannot be written loses the row, not the change
items.body:
Every administrative change writes a row describing it, and that row is written after the change has already reached disk. An unreachable trail is therefore an unwritten row and nothing more: the change stands, the verb reports its own outcome rather than the trail's, and bookkeeping does not reverse work that already happened. Whether an act succeeded and whether it could be recorded are separate answers, which matters because they need opposite responses from you.

The two places that answer is worth the most are the two where the wrong reading destroys something. Generating a signing key writes the sealed private key first and the selector row second, so a refusal read as `the selector was never added` would erase the key it had just written and leave the selector published: a domain signing nothing and failing alignment on everything it sends. And restoring from a backup sets the old data directory aside, moves the bundle in, opens the result and verifies its chain before reporting success, so a refusal read as `the volume did not open` would roll the recovery back. An operator recovering from an outage is the very person whose audit sink is most likely to be unavailable, which makes that the worst available moment to lose one.

Both restore verbs say so on standard error and still exit zero, because the volume that would have held that row is the one just replaced and nothing else on the machine carries the fact. They say it in two sentences rather than one, because the two failures leave you different work: the row could not be written at all, or the row was written and could not be settled onto the volume, in which case the trail may carry it after all. Rows are written before the verb returns rather than buffered, so this costs no durability, and a deletion that has to be provable is unaffected: a deletion is additionally recorded by the framework's own erasure path.

items.title: The administration surface records what it refused and what it canceled
items.body:
Two things a console does are only worth anything if you can read them back afterwards, and both are on the trail.

An account that does not administer this server is turned away from every administration page and every administration form, and that refusal is recorded, naming the account and the exact verb it asked for. A signed-in mailbox owner working through the console by hand is the event an incident is reconstructed from, and it is the stronger signal of the two: a caller with no session at all leaves a row of the framework's own, while this one names somebody who is already inside.

Canceling a queued message erases it from the volume, so the trail is where the answer lives. The queue page asks why, records a row per canceled message naming you, the message, the recipient it was for, your reason and whether the sender was written to, and files it under the same name the `blamepost queue` command uses, so one filter finds both. It also does not act on a message it no longer holds. Selecting a message that has since gone out, ended in a report, or been canceled from another window says so rather than reporting a cancellation, because telling an operator working through a compromised account's outbound mail that a message is gone when it is not is the one answer this page must never give.

items.title: A signing key that will not open names its domain and its selector, and signs nothing
items.body:
Every DKIM private key is sealed on the data volume, and three things leave one unusable: the file is not there, it is there and carries no seal, or it is there and does not open. Signing runs on every message an account submits, so each of those is answered where an operator can act on it. The refusal names the domain, the selector and the algorithm, says which of the three it met, and prints the way out with the pair's selector already filled in: restore the volume from a backup taken before it happened, or retire the pair and mint a replacement. A key that opens for nobody here was either written under a different volume's vault key or damaged where it lies, and those two are indistinguishable from the outside, so the refusal names both rather than choosing one. A passphrase that does not fit is neither and never reaches this point, because it stops the server at start.

A file carrying no seal is refused rather than signed with. This server seals every private key it writes, so a key file that is not sealed was put there by something else and has been readable to anyone who could read the volume for as long as it has been there. That refusal says to treat the pair as exposed and to withdraw its records immediately rather than after the usual overlap.

None of the three carries the data directory, the key filename scheme or any part of the volume's layout, because a refusal the signer writes is one an administration page is allowed to show word for word; these three reach the log and the audit trail, since signing happens on the send path rather than on a page. Mail from the domain still relays unsigned meanwhile, since a key problem is not a reason to refuse an account's own mail. The reason it went unsigned is recorded under a code you can filter on, and is told apart from a domain that simply has no keys yet.

items.title: Mail sent from the browser or over JMAP leaves the same trail as mail sent over submission
items.body:
A message that could not be signed still goes out, because a key problem is not a reason to refuse an account's own mail, so the audit row is the only place that fact ever surfaces. That makes the row's outcome load-bearing: it is what you filter on while working out why a domain's DMARC reports have started arriving, and a send filed as a success would answer with the opposite of what happened.

So every surface that composes a message files the same thing: a failure, naming the domain, carrying the signer's code in a field of its own, and split across two names so a domain still waiting for its first key pair is not filed as one whose key has gone. `blamepost audit read --action blamepost.mail.compose.unsigned_no_key` finds the first and `--action blamepost.mail.compose.unsigned` the second, beside the two names the submission listener already writes, and mail submitted over JMAP files under that same pair, since it is composed here rather than on the submission port. An alert wants all four names. A line naming the domain also goes to the log as the message leaves, so a fault you are already watching for does not wait to be asked about.

items.title: Every RSA DKIM selector this server mints is 2048 bits
items.body: 2048 is the current DKIM key-strength guidance and the 2024 bulk-sender floor, and it is what every RSA selector minted here gets. There is no setting that lowers it: the size is not an environment variable or a configuration key, and the signer refuses to be built at all below the floor rather than carrying a smaller number down to the key generator and relaying whatever the generator says about its own options. The framework underneath still admits 1024 as an opt-in; nothing here takes it.

items.title: A sealed key that will not open has two causes, and the passphrase is not one of them
items.body:
A sealed TLS private key that will not open cannot mean the passphrase has changed, and the certificate report does not send you to check it. The passphrase opens the vault while the server is starting, and one that does not fit stops the boot right there, so any read that runs at all is running under a passphrase that fitted. Checking it would cost an afternoon on the one thing already proven correct.

So the report names the two causes that are left. The file was written under a different volume's vault key, or its bytes have been damaged where they lie. Restore it from a backup taken from before the damage, or write the unsealed pair to the two paths this server reads.

The browser surface takes the same key through the same seal on its way to binding the TLS port, and refuses in those same words, so the sentence you read does not depend on which of the two showed it to you.

items.title: The console names what it is about to destroy and asks you to type it back
items.body:
Five acts on the administration pages cannot be taken back from those pages: archiving an account, withdrawing a hosted domain, removing an alias, retiring a signing pair, and canceling messages off the outbound queue. Each of them is one button on a list of rows that all look alike, and a row is chosen with a mouse.

So each of them takes two posts. The first changes nothing and answers with a page naming exactly what is about to happen and what it reaches. The second has to carry a value read off that page and typed back: the account's address, the domain name, the alias address (or the domain, where the alias is a catch-all), the selector, or how many of the messages you picked are still waiting. A page cannot supply that on your behalf, which is the whole difference between a confirmation and a hidden field, and none of it is a dialog the browser puts up: a browser can be told to stop showing those and nothing about one reaches the server, so this is checked here, against state read here.

The count is the one that does more than slow you down. It is measured again at the moment of the act, so a message that reaches its recipient, ends in a report, or is canceled from another window between the two posts no longer matches, and nothing is erased under a page that has gone stale.

The reversible acts do not ask you to type anything back, deliberately, because a console that asked for a typed value on everything teaches an operator to type through the question, which is the same as not asking. Suspending an account, putting a domain back in service, and giving or taking back the operator role each ask for the reason they record and nothing more. Reinstating an account, adding a domain or an alias, minting and rotating a pair, withdrawing selectors whose overlap has already run out, and forcing the queue change on one press. An archived account carries the button that reinstates it, so the list offers the way back rather than leaving one off by omission.

items.title: The reason an administrative row records is the one the operator typed
items.body:
Suspending an account, archiving one, withdrawing a domain, removing an alias and canceling a queued message each write an audit row with a reason column of its own, and that column is what somebody reading the trail afterwards has to go on. Each of them asks the operator for it and refuses without one in the layer that performs the act rather than in the browser, so that layer is the authority on whether it may proceed. Canceling a queued message carries a second demand of the same kind: the spool's own remove verb also refuses a caller that has not said whether the sender of the canceled message is written to, so no surface can settle that by leaving it out.

A form that filled the column in on the operator's behalf would be worse than one that left it empty. A reason that is present and identical on every row reads like somebody wrote it, so a trail full of them answers nothing while looking as though it does, and an absent one is at least visibly absent. Where a verb genuinely warrants no typed reason, the layer performing it records its own account of the run instead: retiring a signing pair records the selectors it retired and the keys it erased, and the signer's own sentence where it refused, rather than a sentence collected by a form and thrown away.

items.title: Canceling queued mail never writes to an address a stranger chose
items.body:
Canceling a message off the outbound queue erases it, so its sender would otherwise be left believing it went out. Which sender gets told depends on which of the two kinds of message it is, and the console tells them apart before it writes to anybody.

A message relayed after an authenticated submission carries a reverse path bound to the account that authenticated, because the submission listener refuses a MAIL FROM the account does not own. That address is a mailbox here and its owner is exactly who needs telling. A message an alias is forwarding off this server is the other kind: its reverse path arrived on the inbound wire, whoever sent the message chose it, and nothing has ever checked it against anything. Reporting to that turns one press of a button into mail from this server to an address somebody else picked, which is backscatter, and the incident runbook sends an operator to this page during exactly the event that fills a queue with it.

The rule is that a report this page generates is only ever addressed to a domain this server hosts, so it is delivered here or refused here and never reaches an address somebody else picked. A reverse path in a hosted domain is written to; anything else is not written to at all, the empty reverse path included, for the reason RFC 5321 section 6.1 gives. The page says which of your selection falls on each side before you confirm, and the row for each canceled message records whether the sender was told, so an operator who does need to reach a legitimate remote sender has the recipient and the reverse path in front of them instead of an assumption that everybody was told.

items.title: The console will not take itself away from every administrator
items.body:
Four forms on the administration pages could leave this server with nobody able to sign in to it: suspending the last administrator, archiving them, taking the operator role from them, and withdrawing the domain that administrator's address belongs to, since an account is only usable while its domain is. Any of the four and the console is shut to everyone, with no way back through the browser, because the administrator role is granted from these pages and there are no pages left to grant it from.

What that costs is more than the mistake looks like. The command line verbs that put an account or a domain back need the data volume, and the running server holds it, so recovering means stopping the server: every listener down and mail queued at the sending side until somebody notices. Each of the four measures who would still be able to sign in afterwards and refuses when the answer is nobody, naming the way forward: give another account the role first, or, for the three that have a host verb, stop the server and run it from there. Taking the role names none, because the console is the only place the role is granted, and naming a verb that does not exist would send you to a terminal to find out. The refusal is recorded whichever way you arrived at it, because somebody reaching for the one action that closes the console is worth reading about afterwards.

It refuses on that reading alone and never on the verb. Suspending an administrator, archiving one, or taking the role back while another administrator remains all go through, and so does withdrawing a domain that holds no administrator, which is what keeps containment available: an account whose password has been taken is closed from the console in the ordinary way as long as you are not the last one left, and from the host with the server stopped when you are. The identity layer carries no check of its own, so `blamepost account suspend` and `blamepost domain disable` refuse nothing here.

The reading is taken in the moment the change is saved rather than when the page was drawn, which is what makes two windows and two operators safe. Each of two changes aimed at the last two administrators reads a server that still has one left, and each is right about a server neither of them is going to leave behind. Whichever arrives second is refused, with the same sentence and the same recorded row as a single change that would strand the console, and the change that arrived first stands. You still meet the refusal early, before you are asked to type an address or a domain name back, so a change that was never going to be allowed costs one press; that early answer is a courtesy rather than the decision.

items.title: One domain name, one meaning, on every surface that reads one
items.body:
A domain reaches this server in more than one spelling and all of them are legitimate. `example.com.` carries the DNS root's trailing dot, which RFC 1035 makes the absolute form of the same name, and `EXAMPLE.COM` differs only in case, which RFC 4343 says is not a difference. Both arrive: from a message header, from a form on the administration pages, from a command line argument, from a configuration file.

Every surface folds the name through one derivation before anything is keyed on it, so a hosted-domain row, the sealed private key file named for a domain, the signer built for that domain, the audit row recording a change to it and the DNS report addressed to it all name the same domain whichever spelling arrived. It matters most where two of those meet: a selector row and the key file it points at are written by different spellings of one name only once, and the second half is then unreachable from the first.

The set port 25 measures every recipient against is read the same way, from the domain rather than from the spelling a stored row happens to hold, so a domain the console lists and the command line reports as hosted is a domain the MX listener accepts mail for. That set is fixed when the listener is built and there is no second chance at it: a hosted domain reaching it as a spelling would have its mail refused as a stranger's, permanently, with nothing above the wire able to see it happen. A stored name that cannot be read as a domain at all stops the boot and names the row, rather than being folded into something and then served.

An SMTP envelope is the one place the absolute form is not a spelling of the name, because RFC 5321 leaves no empty label at the end of a domain. A `MAIL FROM` or `RCPT TO` carrying the root dot is refused where it is read, as an address this server could not parse rather than as a domain it does not host, and that difference is what the sending side acts on. Message headers, command line arguments and stored rows all take the absolute form and fold it.

The distinction the derivation draws is between a name this server is and a name a zone answers with. The first is folded and used to key things. The second is folded only far enough to be compared, and is never refused on its shape, because a record that is wrong in a hostile way is exactly the one `blamepost doctor` has to tell you about.

A name that only renders like a domain you host is refused rather than folded into a near-match. A label containing raw Unicode, a label already encoded as `xn--`, and a label mixing scripts are each turned away at every entry point, so a lookalike cannot become a second hosted domain, a second selector row or a second key file. What comes back is this server's own refusal naming the rule that rejected the name, rather than a message written for whoever composed the framework underneath it.

An address carries a domain, so the same spellings arrive inside one. Nothing on the wire reads a message header against the envelope grammar, so a message whose `From` or `To` names `bob@EXAMPLE.NET.` is accepted, filed and readable like any other, and it sits in a mailbox for as long as its owner keeps it. Answering it derives the mailbox rather than measuring the bytes, so a reply, a forward and a JMAP submission built from that header all send. What leaves carries the derived name in the header and in the envelope both, which is a forward path the next server along reads under the same grammar this one refuses the other spelling for. A subaddress tag stays attached, because it belongs to the mailbox the sender chose rather than to this server, and a recipient's filter still sees the address they handed out.

A credential names an address too, and every listener that takes one answers about the mailbox rather than about the spelling. Submission, IMAP, POP3 and ManageSieve each sign an account in whichever way its domain was written in the client's configuration, so a client configured with `EXAMPLE.COM` is not locked out of a mailbox at `example.com`. None of the four turns a spelling into a second identity: a POP3 session holding a maildrop refuses another spelling of the same account as the maildrop being held rather than opening a second view of it, and a ManageSieve session opened by any spelling lists that account's own scripts. A name that only renders like the hosted one is refused on all four.

A setting that names an address is folded the same way, so what a configuration file holds and the mailbox it names are one string, and a `security.txt` contact written with the root dot is the valid URI it is rather than a boot failure. So is the destination a receiver publishes for its TLS reports: the report is addressed to the derived name, so a receiver that published the absolute form is one this server can still deliver to.

items.title: Four independent ways to verify the release you are about to run
items.body: SSH-signed commits and tags, SLSA L3 provenance, Sigstore-keyless signatures over both software bills of materials, and byte digests over SHA-256 and SHA3-512 alongside an ML-DSA-65 sidecar signature. Each is checkable without trusting the other three, and SECURITY.md carries the exact commands. One half of the fourth is not live yet: the sidecar appears from the first release cut after the release-signing key is set up, and until then the workflow step that would write it produces no signature and says why in a warning annotation, while that root's byte digests and the three roots before it ship as usual. The step reports as having succeeded rather than as skipped, so what tells you the sidecar was not written is the annotation and the missing file rather than the step's own status. A release carrying no sidecar file is that, rather than a sign of tampering. keys/allowed_signers ships in the repository so tag verification works offline, which also means it arrives with the tag it is being used to check: SECURITY.md records the fingerprint to compare it against and names the source outside this repository that confirms it.

items.title: Building the image never uploads your credentials, wherever in the tree they sit
items.body: The compose stack reads the vault passphrase out of `.env` and documents a local `docker build` from that same directory, so the file that seals every key on your data volume is sitting in the build context. `.dockerignore` is not `.gitignore`: its patterns are matched against the whole relative path with a wildcard that never crosses a directory separator, so a bare name there covers the context root and nothing underneath it. Every exclusion this repository ships is written `**/name`, which covers the root and every directory below it, and that holds for environment files, private keys, certificates, gate logs, editor state and local data directories alike. One re-include sits last, because the last matching line decides a path, and it names a certificate shape rather than a subtree: the vendored framework carries a trust anchor whose extension is on the credential list, so that file comes back and nothing else under `lib/vendor/` does. Written as a subtree it would cancel every exclusion above it for everything below that prefix, and the environment file, private key and registry configuration withheld everywhere else would be uploaded from there and shipped inside the image, since the runtime stage copies `lib` whole. As it stands the image is built from a tree matching the one lib/vendor/MANIFEST.json pins. A build renders the context with Docker itself and checks what arrived, at the root and one directory in, rather than reading the patterns and trusting them.

items.title: The DANE refusal points at the requirement it is enforcing
items.body: `outboundPolicy.dane: "enforce"` needs `outboundPolicy.dnssecValidated: true` beside it, because nothing on this server can tell whether the resolver it was handed validates DNSSEC, and authenticating a peer against a TLSA record nobody validated is worse than not running DANE. The refusal, the settings reference and the operator guide all cite RFC 7672 §2.1.1 and §2.2, where the specification requires a security-aware resolver and confines DANE authentication to records obtained from a DNSSEC-validated lookup, so checking the citation lands you on the requirement rather than on the background that motivates it.

items.title: A DKIM private key never outlives the record that named it
items.body:
Withdrawing a hosted domain, or a single selector, moves the sealed private key out of its place before the record goes and destroys it once the record has. The order is the guarantee. A selector record's key file name is the only thing on the serving path that can find that file: nothing walks the `keys` folder in the course of running, and a backup copies the whole data volume, so a key left behind would sign mail as the domain for the life of the volume and of every copy of it, including after the name is hosted somewhere else.

Three ways out, and they need different things from you. A key the volume will not move refuses the whole withdrawal with the record intact, so running the command again reaches it. A key that moved and could not then be destroyed is left in the `keys` folder under a name no record points at, and no second run finds it: the command names it and you delete it by hand. And a key that moved and could not be put back sits under its own name with `.erasing` on the end, with nothing under the name the record points at: running the withdrawal again puts it back before it stages it a second time, and renaming it back by hand first reaches the same place. What refuses instead is a folder holding both names at once, which is that leftover plus a key minted since, because staging the new one renames it onto the leftover and the leftover is the only copy there is. `blamepost doctor` reports the two outcomes that leave a file, under `signing keys`, and it is the reader that holds that folder against the published records. `blamepost dkim sweep --immediate` withdraws a record before its overlap has elapsed, which is what to reach for when you believe a key is exposed, and it destroys any private key still sitting behind that record for the same reason; on the ordinary rotation path `blamepost dkim retire` has already destroyed the pair's private halves a step earlier, so what the sweep takes is the record.

items.title: A withdrawal decides against the volume it is standing on, not the one it started on
items.body:
Destroying signing material is the only thing `domain remove` and a selector withdrawal wait on, so the refusals that decide whether the records may go are settled in one uninterruptible step, with the key material already moved out of its place and still able to go back, immediately before the records are deleted. An unreadable argument, a domain this server does not host and a volume opened for reporting are all answered before that step opens and before any key is touched; what is settled inside it is the part that another process can change while the withdrawal is running. A refusal costs nothing: the keys return to where they were, byte for byte, and the domain is exactly as it was. That is what answers the two things which can arrive while a withdrawal is running. An account created on the domain keeps the domain, and the domain keeps the keys its published records name. A selector published on it is not dropped, because dropping the records for a set whose keys were never touched would leave the newest key on the volume with nothing able to name it. Both say why and both can simply be run again.

The refusal that keeps a domain able to sign is settled in that same step, and it is a statement about every selector the domain signs with rather than about the one being withdrawn. Two withdrawals running at once, each taking one half of the only pair a domain has, each see the other half still signing until the moment it stops; whichever reaches the deletion second is refused and its key goes back. A domain is never left with no active selector at all, and the check is made against the set the domain still signs with at the moment the row is deleted rather than the set the withdrawal read when it started.

One outcome leaves work, and it is named where it happens rather than left in the trail. A key that was moved out of its place and could not be destroyed once its records had gone is sitting in the `keys` folder under a name no record points at, so nothing signs with it and nothing on the serving path will find it again: `domain remove` and `dkim sweep` each print the name and the audit row carries it, and `blamepost doctor` lists it afterwards under `signing keys`. Delete it by hand. A later withdrawal that would have to write over one of those refuses instead, because what is sitting there is signing material and a rename onto it destroys the one copy that exists.

items.title: The operator role is granted only to a mailbox that can use it
items.body:
The console gives the operator role only to an account that is in service. `store.accounts.setAdmin` refuses a grant to a mailbox that is suspended, archived or part way through an erasure, and the sentence it refuses with names which of the three it met and what to do about it. The account list offers the button that grants the role on an active row alone, so the two agree, and the refusal sits in the layer that performs the act rather than only in the page that offers it.

What is asked is whether the mailbox can present a credential, not which way out of service it took, because none of the three can. A role written onto one of them is inert the day it lands and still reads as an administrator wherever administrators are listed, so somebody counting who administers this server finds an account that cannot sign in and has to work out whether that is a mistake or a containment nobody finished. Two of the three also come back on purpose. A suspension is the hold an operator applies to a mailbox whose password may be in somebody else's hands, and it is lifted deliberately, so a role granted during one would be waiting the moment the account is trusted again; archiving is reversible the same way, and the role would return with the mailbox without anybody having decided that it should. Reinstate the account first where the role is meant to be there. A status this server gains later is refused here as well rather than let through by not having been named. What the refusal reads is the state the volume recorded, so an erasure that could write neither the status nor the mark beside it leaves an account nothing can tell apart from one in service; `blamepost account remove --destroy` says so when that happens, and suspending the account is what closes it.

Taking the role back is not gated on status at all, and the account list carries that button on any row holding the role whatever its status says. One refusal does meet it, and it is not about the mailbox: the console will not let you revoke the last account holding the role, and there is no command-line verb that does it instead. Revocation is the containment the verb exists for, so gating it would strand the role on exactly the accounts nothing else can reach to lift it off: an archived account cannot be suspended to get at the role another way, and one part way through an erasure can neither be suspended nor returned to service at all.

items.title: A sender that trickles a message is cut instead of holding a connection
items.body:
A peer sending a message body slower than a hundred bytes a second is answered `421 4.7.0` and disconnected, on both SMTP listeners, and on the submission listener whether the body arrives through `DATA` or `BDAT`. The idle timeout cannot bound this: a peer sending one byte at a time is never idle, so each arrival pushes the deadline out again, and the connection is held for as long as the peer likes along with its share of the per-address ceiling. The rate is judged over short windows rather than averaged across the whole transfer, so an opening burst buys no credit against an arbitrarily slow tail. A hundred bytes a second is orders of magnitude below what a working sender achieves on a bad link, so ordinary mail is nowhere near the floor.

The floor is on the two SMTP listeners and nowhere else. An IMAP `APPEND` literal and a ManageSieve `PUTSCRIPT` upload are bounded by the idle timeout alone, which the same trickle pushes out one byte at a time, so a client that has authenticated can hold one of those connections for as long as it likes. Both take an authenticated session to reach, which is what leaves them to the per-address ceiling rather than to a rate floor.

items.title: Each listener holds a ceiling of its own, not only one per address
items.body:
Every mail listener accepts at most 1024 sockets at once, whoever they belong to: five of them on the default configuration, six with POP3 turned on. The per-address ceilings bound one peer and say nothing about how many peers there are, so without this the process-wide total is the per-address number multiplied by however many source addresses a caller can speak from, which a botnet, a NAT pool or a single IPv6 /64 makes large. Every accepted socket costs a descriptor and a parser before anything authenticates, so a socket over the ceiling is closed before the connection handler sees it. Every listener releases a peer that drops the connection itself and not only one the server ends, so an unauthenticated peer cannot grow the live-connection set by connecting and hanging up.

Two things to know before you go looking for it. The number is not a setting: no configuration this server reads widens or narrows it, while the per-address ceiling is yours to set and reaches 1024 at its own maximum, which is one source address able to take a whole listener. And a socket dropped at the ceiling gets a bare close with no protocol line, no log and no audit row, where a per-address refusal writes all three, so a listener sitting at its ceiling looks from the trail like a listener nobody is calling. The browser and JMAP ports are not in this at all and hold no such ceiling.

items.title: The decrypted working copy is refused rather than guessed onto disk
items.body: The database is encrypted at rest, so reading it means writing a decrypted copy somewhere, and that somewhere has to be memory. This server asks the kernel which filesystem is mounted at the candidate directory rather than trusting the name to mean what it usually means: a host or image carrying `/dev/shm` as an ordinary directory is refused, and so is any platform with no such mount at all. The refusal names the mount it wanted, the variable to set, and off Linux the platform that has no such mount. Nothing infers a memory-backed mount from a path existing, on any platform, so the default path puts no plaintext database on persistent storage. Naming a directory with `BLAMEJS_TMPDIR` is judged on weaker evidence. On Linux the path is resolved and has to sit under `/dev/shm`, `/run/shm`, `/run/user` or `/tmp`, and anything outside those four is refused at boot under `db/tmpdir-not-tmpfs`; that is a comparison against four names rather than a reading of the mount table, so a directory under `/tmp` is accepted on the strength of its name and puts the decrypted database on disk wherever `/tmp` is a disk. Off Linux no mount can be classified at all, the directory you name is used, and the only signal is a warning naming it. Treat whatever you point it at as carrying the same secrets the volume does, and keep it out of your backups, replicas and disk images.

items.title: A queue descriptor is written only once the message is on the volume
items.body: Writing a waiting recipient to the outbound queue puts the message on the volume first and the descriptor that names it second, so that an interrupted write leaves a message nobody has to send yet rather than a descriptor with nothing behind it, which the sweep would clear and the message would be gone. A descriptor write the volume refuses is followed by an attempt to take the message back off the volume, and the failure reaches the sender either way, so the recipient is not spooled and the sender keeps their copy. A volume that will not take the descriptor may not take the removal either; that leaves the body where it is, and the server logs the id along with the two commands that reach it. What no cleanup can cover is a process that stops between the two writes, so the queue also reconciles. `blamepost doctor` holds the bodies on disk against the descriptors and names up to five that nothing claims, passing over any written in the last five minutes, since a body that new is more likely to be a spool in progress than a stranded one. `blamepost queue list` reports how much of the ceiling they are holding and names every one of them, with the ids to clear them by.

items.title: A deleted filter script leaves nothing of itself on the volume
items.body:
A Sieve script names the correspondents its owner sorts on and the addresses they forward to, so its name and its body are stored sealed. Deleting one removes it rather than unlinking it: the database is opened with SQLite's secure delete, so the content a delete frees is overwritten instead of being left in the page until some later write happens to reuse the slot. The same holds for an annotation a client clears and an alias you remove, each of which carries sealed columns of its own. A domain row is the exception worth knowing: the only column sealed on it is who acknowledged its DNS, because the name itself is published in DNS by definition, so withdrawing a domain has no sealed name to dispose of.

What the property reaches is the decrypted working copy, and it reaches it at the next flush. The encrypted database on the volume is rewritten on a timer, on close and on exit, and until the flush after a delete that file still holds the whole database as it stood before it, openable by anyone holding the passphrase. The rewrite replaces the file rather than editing it, so the blocks the previous copy occupied are released to the filesystem rather than overwritten, and a snapshot, a replica or a backup taken before the delete is untouched by any of this. Retiring those copies is yours to do.

items.title: Every listener names the key agreements it accepts, and puts them in an order
items.body:
Every port that terminates TLS presents a context carrying a key-agreement preference rather than taking whatever the runtime happens to offer: the six mail listeners and the browser port on 8443. Port 8080 is cleartext and has no context to carry one. All of them also advertise RFC 8879 certificate compression, so the certificate stops being the largest thing on the wire during a handshake. The preference is a run of positions separated by slashes, and every group this server prefers holds a position of its own: X25519MLKEM768, then SecP256r1MLKEM768, then SecP384r1MLKEM1024, then X25519. Ordering exists only between positions, so two groups sharing one stop being ranked against each other and a hybrid packed in beside X25519 would lose to it whenever a peer offered both; a position per group is the only shape that means what the list says. The last position is the exception and holds the remaining curves RFC 8446 §4.2.7 registers, X448, secp256r1, secp384r1 and secp521r1, as one set with no preference between them, because they are there so a conforming peer is never refused rather than to be chosen. What the tuple form buys is the retry: a peer that names a hybrid anywhere in what it offers is asked to try again on the hybrid even when it put a classical curve first, and only a peer implementing no hybrid at all completes on a classical curve. That behavior belongs to the TLS library reading the string rather than to anything this server does afterwards, and no test here observes it, so `openssl s_client -trace` against a port is what confirms it on your build. Nothing records which group ran: the runtime reports a negotiated group on an outbound connection and not on an accepted one.

The eight groups above are the whole accept set, so what a peer offering only something else meets is a refused handshake. Of the groups RFC 8446 §4.2.7 registers, the only ones left off are the finite-field Diffie-Hellman parameters; a peer that offers only a brainpool TLS 1.3 curve, secp256k1 or a hybrid codepoint this server does not publish is refused as well. That matters because no listener accepts an envelope on an unencrypted session: a sender refused at the handshake on port 25 retries in the clear, is answered 530 5.7.0 Must issue a STARTTLS command first, and its message stays in its own queue rather than arriving unencrypted. A group left off costs whole messages, so everything a conforming implementation is required to carry is in the set: RFC 8446 §9.1 makes secp256r1 mandatory and X25519 only a SHOULD, and both are accepted, along with secp384r1, secp521r1 and X448. What is refused is what such a peer never offers on its own. The browser interface carries the same preference, so testing the administration URL and testing port 25 give the same answer about the key agreement, and the operator guide carries openssl commands for checking a sender that cannot complete a handshake.

items.title: A reporting command cannot write, rather than promising not to
items.body:
The verbs that answer while the server is running open the volume read-only, and read-only is enforced by the database handle rather than by each verb remembering. A write that reaches it fails at the statement, so a path that gained one by mistake refuses instead of succeeding into a working copy nobody persists. The encrypted database, the sealed database key, the audit checkpoints and the record of where the audit chain was last anchored are all left byte for byte as they were, and the decrypted working copy is removed when the command returns.

`blobs reclaim` refuses on that open outright, and this is the one case where a reporting command could still have destroyed mail. Unlinking a message body is a filesystem call, so no database setting could stop it: run against rows that stopped at the server's last write to disk, it would delete bodies on the live volume while every message delivered since went unaccounted for, and the audit row that is the only record those bodies existed could not be written at all. Stop the server to reclaim. The same rule holds for the verbs that destroy a domain's sealed signing keys.

A reader takes no lock and waits for none, because it is not a second writer: the refusal that keeps two processes from writing one volume exists to stop them overwriting each other's copy of it, and a command that never writes has nothing to lose that race with.

The read-only open is the fallback, not the default. Each of these verbs asks for the volume the ordinary way first and takes the read-only path only when the running server already holds it, so against a stopped server the same command opens for writing, takes the volume lock, and anchors the audit chain on its way in. `blamepost doctor` on a stopped server is therefore a command that writes, and the byte-for-byte guarantee above is a statement about the fallback. Nine verbs may take that fallback: `account list` and `account show`, `domain list` and `domain show`, `dkim list` and `dkim records`, `blobs report`, `audit verify-chain`, and `doctor`. Everything else waits for the server to stop.

items.title: An erasure reports every record it could not destroy, and never ends on one
items.body:
An account erasure destroys six kinds of record an account holds, and each one is refused separately. The delete path answers per message and consults both the preservation-order register and the retention floor. The hard erase under the mailbox rows, the filter scripts and the annotations consults the governance gate per row and nothing else, because an order is placed against a message and none of those three can be one. The aliases and the account row itself are the other two, and they carry their own name into the register, which holds no order over either. All six come back in one report and the command always finishes rather than ending on the first refusal, which matters because by the time any of them is reached the mail is already destroyed. Each entry names the record rather than the table it was in, gives the reason it stayed, and says whether something is deliberately keeping it or something went wrong with it, which are the two cases that need opposite responses from you.

The audit row is written on every path, with a count of what went and what stayed, and it records the destruction as a failure only when something that was not kept on purpose could not be erased. So an erasure that half ran is answerable: the request has a record, and the account holder can be told what happened to their mail.

The command prints the same distinction. A record held back on purpose is a `kept` line and leaves the exit status 0; one that could not be erased for any other reason is a `FAIL` line and exits 1, so a script driving a bulk erasure stops on the account that needs a person. A mailbox row a governance gate is holding is a `kept` line rather than a fault, and you are told to run the erasure again only while the identity it names is still there to run it against.

The report counts messages apart from the mailbox rows, filter scripts and annotations that stayed, so a count of a subject's surviving mail is a count of mail. `mailPreserved` and `mailFailed` carry messages; `recordsPreserved` and `recordsFailed` carry everything else. Every record that stayed is still named individually, whichever kind it is, and the two sentences sending you to look for message content on the volume are printed only for messages.

items.title: A preservation order covers the messages it names, and the guide says what it does not
items.body:
The register behind `blamepost account hold` is keyed on the exact record an order is placed against, and what the command places one against is a message. So an order over an account's mail preserves those messages on every protocol and in an account erasure, and it does not extend to that account's filter scripts, its annotations or its aliases: an erasure run while the order stands keeps every message it covers and destroys all three. The account row survives with them, because a kept message is addressable only through it, and the erasure is reported as the partial one it is.

The operator guide and the hardening checklist state that boundary, with what to do instead. Where a matter requires the fact that an address existed, or the rules its owner filtered on, hold the erasure until the matter closes; there is no wider order to place, and one this server cannot record is worse than none because you would believe it was in force. `blamepost account holds <address>` remains the way to establish what is actually covered rather than trusting the command that placed it.

items.title: A canceled message is one this server erased, and nothing else is reported as one
items.body:
Canceling a selection off the outbound queue works through it one message at a time, and each message is checked against the spool in the moment it is canceled rather than once for the whole selection. A message that reaches its recipient partway through is reported as not canceled, is left out of the count, and files an audit row under `blamepost.mail.queue.message_removed` with outcome `failure` saying it was not erased.

Its sender is not written to. A cancellation sends a delivery report to the reverse path, and a message that arrived through a forwarding alias carries a reverse path whoever sent it chose, so a report about a message that was in fact delivered is both untrue and mail this server sends to an address a stranger picked. The queue page says that some of your selection was canceled and some was not, without naming which, and tells you to read the queue again; the distinction an incident turns on is in that reading and on the audit trail, and anything reported as gone is to be treated as delivered.

`blamepost queue remove` answers the same way, and has the same window to cross: it reads the queue, opens the data volume, and erases. Opening the volume unseals the vault and decrypts the database, and `blamepost queue flush` and the running server both send mail without telling that command, so the message can leave inside it. The id is checked again immediately before the erasure, and one that has gone is refused with a non-zero status saying nothing was removed. The recorded row carries the `failure` verdict and the reason you gave, so the moment you asked is still in the trail. An id that names nothing at all is still refused before the volume is opened, which keeps a typo an argument error rather than a lock the running server is holding.

items.title: A message refused by a full outbound queue has not reached anybody
items.body:
Room for everything a message will need is taken when its recipients are known and before the first copy is filed anywhere, and it is held until the message is finished with. A temporary code on a full queue therefore means nothing arrived: not in a mailbox on this server, not in the queue. The sender still holds the whole message, and sending it again delivers one copy rather than a second copy to everyone who already had it. That applies to a mixed envelope naming both a mailbox here and a recipient elsewhere, on submission and on port 25 alike, and to an address on a hosted domain that forwards off this server, whose outbound entry is counted as the entry it is.

Because the room is held rather than measured, two connections crossing the last slot together cannot both pass: the second is answered with a temporary code, which is the honest answer, and the queue stays inside the ceiling `BLAMEPOST_OUTBOUND_SPOOL` sets. The count of what is held lives in the process holding it, so it bounds the running server against itself; a second process draining the same queue measures the directory rather than that count.

A server near its ceiling can refuse while `blamepost queue list` still shows a slot free, for two reasons worth telling apart. A slot spoken for by a message in flight is not on disk yet and comes back when that message finishes. And mail arriving from strangers is admitted against a share of the ceiling rather than the whole of it, as are the reports this server generates, while `queue list` prints the whole ceiling; so forwarding is refused at a lower number than that line shows.

items.title: A mint never writes over a sealed private key that is already on the volume
items.body:
A DKIM key file is named from the domain, the selector and the algorithm, so two mints asked for the same selector arrive at the same file name. The material is written before the record naming it, because a published record for a key that is not there is a domain whose mail leaves unsigned, and until that record lands neither mint can see the other. `blamepost dkim generate` and `blamepost dkim rotate` take the file name in a single exclusive create before writing anything under it. Whichever run loses is refused under `dkim/key-file-held` having written nothing, and the run that won keeps its own key and its own record.

The same refusal covers a key file left behind by a run that stopped between writing the file and publishing the record. Nothing signs with it, `blamepost doctor` reports it under `signing keys` as a key no record names, and minting again for that selector refuses and names the file rather than destroying the only copy of it. The refusal cannot tell that case from a mint in flight, because the record that would say which is the one that has not been written: wait and run `blamepost dkim list`, or delete the named file, or pass `--selector` with a name of your own. A refused mint leaves the domain signing with whatever it was signing with. A mint writes both halves of a pair, so a collision on the second one has a first half already on the volume with a record naming it; that half is retired, its record removed and its key destroyed before the refusal is raised, and where the volume will not take one of those back the refusal names the half that stayed instead of the file it collided with.

items.title: Suspending a mailbox takes effect against a message already arriving
items.body:
Whether a recipient still has somewhere to land is decided at the moment the copy would be filed, rather than when the recipient was accepted at `RCPT TO`. A mailbox you suspend, or a domain you take out of service, while a message is being transmitted does not receive that message. Other recipients on the same message are delivered as usual and nothing is filed into the mailbox you just closed, and the address that closed is answered for with `4.2.1` in a delivery report naming it, wherever the message had another recipient that still landed. A domain you remove outright is a different answer, `5.1.2`, because the server does not handle mail for that name at all.

Where nothing landed, the whole handoff is refused and the peer is answered `451 4.3.0` at the end of `DATA` rather than told which address closed. That is a temporary code, so a message arriving over port 25 for that address alone stays with the peer that sent it and is tried again; the reason word is on the audit trail rather than on the wire. An authenticated submission gets a delivery report either way, whether or not any of its recipients landed.

This is the case that matters, because suspending an account over what is arriving in it is done while mail is in flight by definition. Both listeners that file mail for a recipient ask the same question through the same path, so the answer does not depend on whether the message arrived on port 25 or through submission. An upload into your own mailbox is not in this: an IMAP `APPEND` and the copy the browser composer files into Sent are written directly, since the mailbox they land in is the one that authenticated.

items.title: A cancellation the data volume refuses is reported as a message still going out
items.body:
Canceling a queued message erases the message body, the descriptor naming it and the claim file guarding it, and a volume can decline to release any of them: a backup walking the directory, a scanner holding a handle, a mount that has gone read-only. The cancellation reports which of four things happened rather than assuming the first. The message was there and is gone. There was nothing under that id, so it left on its own and is past canceling. The volume kept a part and nothing at all was destroyed, in which case the message is still queued and the running server will attempt it again on its own schedule. Or part of the entry went and part of it stayed, which is not a cancellation to run again: what went is gone, the message can never be sent, and a second run reaches only the remainder.

The last two are separated because an operator's next move differs, and separating them takes the same claim on the entry that a delivery attempt takes. A cancellation holds the claim across the whole removal where it can take it, which is what lets it put the message back when the descriptor will not go. A delivery attempt already holding that claim does not stop the cancellation, but it does take the restore away from it, so a descriptor refusal there reports `incomplete` rather than `refused`. In the ordinary case: the body is held in memory in front of the first unlink and written again if the second act refuses, so the pair is whole, the sweep still has something to send, and the remediation the refusal names is a real one. Without the claim that restore races the attempt running on the same entry, and between them the two leave a message body no descriptor names. With it, `refused` means strictly that nothing was destroyed and `incomplete` means part of it was.

Only the first outcome is reported as a cancellation. `blamepost queue remove` answers either failure with a non-zero status naming the part that could not be removed and what the volume said, and files an audit row under `blamepost.mail.queue.message_removed` with outcome `failure` carrying the same. The administration queue page leaves the message out of its count, says plainly that not everything was canceled, and writes what the volume refused to the server log. In both places the message's sender is written to only when the message was actually erased, so nobody is sent a delivery report saying an operator stopped mail that is still on its way, and the row records which of the two silences it was: `message-not-cancelled` where nothing left the volume, and `message-destroyed-in-part` where the message went and the entry beside it stayed, so there were no headers left to quote back. Recording the second as the first would say this server did not cancel a message whose body it had already destroyed.

The message body is released before the descriptor that names it, and a body the volume keeps stops the removal there. That leaves the pair whole and still listed, which is the truthful state, rather than a message with nothing describing it that the next retry would write back into the queue.

items.title: A TLS failure observed while a report is being composed is not discarded
items.body:
This server accumulates one file per receiving domain recording how its transport security with that domain actually went, and that file is the only place those observations exist. The daily reporting run takes a file off the volume in three situations: the accumulator holds nothing, the record inside disagrees with the domain it is filed under, and a report it sent accounted for everything the file held. A receiver that publishes no TLS-RPT record is handled differently, and the difference is the point of this: what that run judged is subtracted, and the file goes only if the subtraction empties it. Each of those decisions has to be reached before the removal is queued behind the writes already in flight for that domain, and delivery continues throughout, so a session that fails in between lands in a file that was judged a moment earlier. Nothing else holds that observation, so a removal acting on the earlier reading would take it with the file, silently: the receiver would never be told and no error would be raised anywhere.

So each removal takes the reading again inside the write it acts in. An accumulator that has gained an observation is kept and reported on the next run. For a receiver that publishes no record, only what that run judged is taken back out, so an observation made while the receiver's zone was being read survives. That matters because a domain that publishes a TLS-RPT record tomorrow is owed what failed today. A run that finds nothing new still clears the file, so a receiver that asked for nothing accumulates nothing.

items.title: A delete the volume will not finish is answered for one message at a time
items.body:
Destroying a message is two acts on the data volume once the gates have let it through: the row binding it to a mailbox goes, and the sealed octets that row names go with it when nothing else points at them. The volume can refuse either one, and a mount that has gone read-only, a permission that changed, a file another process holds open, or write-once triggers under a records-retention posture all refuse below the server entirely. A delete of several messages is a set of separate outcomes and each is answered for on its own, so the messages behind a refused one still go rather than being abandoned with their store rows already destroyed.

A message whose storage stayed is reported as one that did not go. Reporting it destroyed would say the octets are gone while they are still on the volume and still readable, and those octets are the message: IMAP BODY[] and POP3 RETR both return them, and they are sealed under the volume's key rather than under anything a row erasure reaches, so one left behind opens exactly as it did before and in every backup taken afterwards.

What the client is told follows its own specification. A POP3 commit answers `-ERR Commit failed: some deleted messages not removed`, with a count per reason and the count that went. JMAP `Email/set` reports the message as one that was not destroyed and carries the reason word, `row-not-removed` or `body-not-removed`, in its description. The browser interface says the removal could not be completed on the data volume and that nothing is keeping the message on purpose, without the reason word, because the reason names work that is the operator's rather than the account holder's. IMAP `EXPUNGE` completes and draws its untagged line, because RFC 9051 gives the command no refusal form and the message really has left the mailbox. An account erasure prints it as a failure rather than as a record kept on purpose, and exits non-zero. None of those replies carries the volume's layout or the message's content digest, because a mailbox protocol owes its client neither; both are on an audit row under `blamepost.mail.mailbox.destruction_incomplete`, which is where an operator reads what is still stored. `blamepost blobs report --verify` accounts for it on the volume, and the two halves end differently: a body left behind with its row gone is reported as one nothing references and `blobs reclaim` frees it once the volume gives the file up, while a row left behind still names its body, so it shows as a quota disagreement and running the delete again is what finishes it.

items.title: A mailbox row outlives every record still bound to it, an annotation included
items.body: An erasure destroys the annotations a client stored on a mailbox before it erases the mailbox row, and it keeps that row when one of them stayed. An annotation carries the opaque token of the mailbox it was set on and no name, so a mailbox row erased out from under one leaves it reachable by nothing at all, and leaves the report of the rerun you were told to run unable to say which of the account's mailboxes the record belonged to. This is the rule the identity layer already applies one level out, where the account row goes only once nothing it holds still names it, applied one level in. `blamepost account remove --destroy` says a mailbox still holds a record this erasure could not destroy, and running the same command again once the gate clears names that mailbox exactly as the first run did.

items.title: A mailbox holds exactly the messages both of its records agree on
items.body:
A message here is two records. The message store keeps one, holding the flags and the sealed subject, correspondents and body; this server keeps the other beside it, holding the unique identifier IMAP hands out and the folder the message is filed in. Membership is decided in one place as the intersection of the two, so `EXISTS`, `FETCH`, `SEARCH`, the POP3 listing and the delete path cannot come to different answers about which messages a mailbox holds, and a row on either side without its partner is left out rather than served half.
