The browser interface and JMAP read the message store directly rather than through that intersection, so a message the store holds and this server never filed is one webmail can render while no folder listing names it, which is the state the reconciliation below exists to close.

The read that decides it asks the store with a bound and raises the bound until the answer comes back short of the bound it was given, because a bounded read that returns exactly as many rows as it was allowed may have been truncated and there is no second field to ask. That matters because the only count this server can set a bound from is its own row count, and the store is entitled to disagree with it. A store row with no partner here shortens such a read by one, and what a shortened read drops is not the unpaired row but whichever paired message the store happens to order last: the mailbox would report fewer messages than it holds, a fetch of everything would return fewer, and a hard delete would answer for a live message with the reason reserved for an identifier that names nothing. Which message disappeared would move as well, because the store orders by modification sequence and a flag change rewrites one, so ordinary use would hide a different message each time. Every read starts from the beginning rather than resuming after the last row of the one before it, because the store assigns one modification sequence to a whole batch of flag changes and a cursor would step over every other row sharing the sequence it stopped on.

The pair can still come apart, and each way it does is named on the trail rather than left to be found. A message written to the store and never filed into a mailbox is one no folder listing names, no delete verb reaches, and an account erasure walks straight past while its subject, its correspondents and its body stay on the volume, so a filing that fails takes the store's row back with it. It does that through the store's own destructive call rather than the delete path, because the retention floor would refuse a message that arrived a moment ago and leave behind exactly the record this exists to remove, and nothing any reader ever had is destroyed: the message reached no mailbox, drew no identifier a client can name, and was never served. Where the store will not give the row back either, the caller still hears why the filing failed and `blamepost.mail.mailbox.filing_not_rolled_back` records what stayed. A move the store completed and this layer could not follow leaves the same shape from the other end, under `blamepost.mail.mailbox.move_unbound`.

The other direction is a row here whose store partner has gone, which is what a destruction the volume half took leaves. Those are finished on the layer that can still see them, with both gates read again rather than assumed settled by the run that stranded the row: a message a preservation order or the retention floor keeps is recorded under `blamepost.mail.mailbox.stranded_preserved`, one that goes under `blamepost.mail.mailbox.stranded_destroyed`, and a row the store can answer for again is handed back rather than destroyed here. The role check in front of the hard delete sits at the head of that path rather than in one branch of it, because a set made entirely of stranded rows never reaches the layer that would otherwise have refused it; a caller without the scope meets the same refusal in the same words either way, recorded under `blamepost.mail.mailbox.expunge_denied`.

items.title: The retention floor measures the arrival this server stamped, never the date a client asked for
items.body:
RFC 9051 section 6.3.12 lets an IMAP client set a message's internal date when it uploads one, so that value arrives from the wire and belongs to whoever wrote it. A floor measured against it would be a floor the client picks: a message uploaded with a date far enough back clears every window an operator can set, and one uploaded with a date ahead of now never leaves. So the regulated minimum is measured against the clock this server stamped when the message was filed, on the ordinary delete path and on the one that finishes a destruction the volume half took alike. The date a client asked for is stored and answered back as `INTERNALDATE`, and the searches RFC 9051 defines over it, `BEFORE`, `ON` and `SINCE`, read that same value, which is what those keys are specified to mean. It reaches one place beyond IMAP, and `blamepost account messages` prints it beside the arrival stamp rather than instead of it. The `arrived` column is the clock reading this server took when it filed the message, and it is what a preservation or erasure answer is built on; the `client` column is the date the message shows, which is what an account holder reads off their own client when they describe a record. Both columns are named, so neither is read for the other.

A row that the finishing path cannot get an arrival time from is kept rather than destroyed. The arithmetic reads an absent arrival as the epoch, which clears every window there is, so the one direction a missing value must not fail in is the one it fails in on its own; that path treats it as inside the window instead. The ordinary path has no such row to meet, because the message store stamps an arrival time on every message it takes. A window only ever elapses, so a message that cleared the floor once still clears it, and what a second reading catches is an operator who has since moved to a stricter posture.

The date a client does supply is refused where it arrives if it is not a moment at all. `mailbox/bad-internaldate` answers an upload carrying a value that is not finite, one before the epoch, or one too large to be held as an exact integer. Each of those survives every later comparison silently: a test against a value that is not a number is false whichever way it is written, and a negative one reads as a message older than any window an operator could set. A field this server answers `INTERNALDATE` from has to hold a date, so it is refused at the point of parse rather than stored and reasoned about afterwards.

items.title: The sign-in form bounds how often it will check a password, and the bound is one count per source address
items.body:
The browser sign-in form accepts fifty posts in any five-minute slot from one source address and answers `429 Too Many Requests` past that until the slot ends. What it bounds is cost rather than guessing: every post buys one password verification, and that verification runs even for an address that has no mailbox here, so that the answer does not say which addresses exist. Guessing at one mailbox is bounded separately, per mailbox, and keyed so that moving to a new source address does not refill it.

This server reads the peer address off the socket and ignores `X-Forwarded-For` everywhere. Behind a TLS terminator, every browser therefore arrives from the terminator's address, and those fifty become one count shared by everyone signing in. Size any front door you put in front of this with that sharing in mind, because a caller can be refused the form having typed nothing wrong. Nothing in the console releases it, since it is not a lockout, and waiting out the slot is the whole remedy.

The refusal is recorded with the route and the peer together, so a row read during an incident says which door was being knocked on rather than only that some machine was refused somewhere.

items.title: Sign-in failure budgets are measured on a clock the host cannot step, and two of them are not
items.body:
The counters this server keeps for sign-in failures are measured on a monotonic reading rather than on the wall clock, so an NTP correction, a virtual machine resuming from a snapshot, or an operator fixing a wrong clock does not release a lockout early or hand back a counter that has not decayed. That covers the per-mailbox guess budget, the per-machine budget, and the thirty-day familiar-source exemption. What an operator reads stays a real date, because the reading is anchored to the wall clock at start and advanced from there rather than translated at the point of display.

Two budgets are not on that clock, and both fail in the permissive direction. The per-source authentication-failure ceiling the mail listeners apply before a password is checked, and the five-minute window on browser sign-in posts, are measured inside the framework, which offers no seam for a clock to be supplied. A step forward past either window ends it early. A host whose time source somebody else can influence therefore has a way to retire those two counts on demand, which makes a disciplined clock part of the posture rather than an operational nicety beside it. Prefer a time source you control.

items.title: The operator console is held to the machine and browser its session was opened on
items.body:
A console session is bound to the client address, the browser, and the accepted language it was opened from. A console request arriving with any of those different is refused and asks for the password again. The session row is kept rather than destroyed, so a stranger replaying a copied cookie cannot sign the operator out by trying, and the account's mail stays open throughout. The page says the console is held to the machine and browser it was opened on; it does not say which of the three differed, because that would tell whoever is holding the cookie which part to fix. The refusal is recorded as `blamepost.web.console_device_refused`.

Mailbox sessions are deliberately not held that way. Binding to the address means a session ends when the address changes, which on a phone moving between wifi and a cell network happens by walking out of a door. A mailbox session used from somewhere new is recorded as `auth.session.fingerprint_drift` and continues, so that action is where to look to see where a mailbox has been signed in from.

The two settings are the trade read in opposite directions. The accounts that reach the console host domains, mint and retire signing keys, cancel queued mail and can read every mailbox on the server, and they are few and mostly at one machine. An operator meeting this spends a password; a copied console cookie that still worked would spend the server.
